iii. Osmosis

It is the diffusion of solvent (water) through a semi-permeable membrane. It is controlled by the relative concentration of solutes in the water on both sides of membrane. Water always moves from a hypotonic solution (with lower concentration of solutes) to a hypertonic solution (with higher concentration of solutes). Few examples of how osmosis occurs in cells are following:
iii. Osmosis

(i) When a cell is placed in a hypotonic solution (which has lower solute concentration than the cell) the rate of movement of water inside the cell is more. In such conditions, animal cells swells and may rupture while the plant cells becomes turgid (due to their hard cell wall).
iii. Osmosis

(ii) When a cell is placed in an isotonic solution (solution in which the concentration of solutes is equal to that of the cell), the rate of osmosis outward is equal to the rate of osmosis to inward. In such a condition, animal cells retain their volume constant while plant cells become flaccid (loose), because the net uptake of water is not enough.
iii. Osmosis

(iii) When a cell is placed in a hypertonic solution (which has higher salt concentration than the cell), water moves out. In such conditions, animal cells shrink in size. In plant cells, the cytoplasm shrinks within the cell wall.
iii. Osmosis
Figure 4.21: Effect of different solutions on animal and plant cells
Scientific Information

When a plant cell loses water, its turgidity is lost and it becomes flaccid (soft and limp). The leaves with flaccid cells become limp and the stem droops. Thus plant cells with reduced turgor are said to be wilting.
Turgor

We know that when a plant cell is surrounded by water or hypotonic solution, the water moves into the cell vacuole by osmosis. The vacuole increases in size and pushes the cell contents against the cell wall. This pressure which is exerted by the cytoplasm against the cell wall is known as turgor pressure and the phenomenon is called turgor.
Turgor
In turgid condition, the plant cell does not burst because the cell wall is strong and relatively inelastic. The importance of turgor in plants are as follows:
Turgor

i) It plays an important role in maintaining the shape of the plant. • ii) It provides supports to plants especially in young tissues. • iii) It also helps in closing and opening of the stomata. • iv) Some flowers open during the day time and close at night. This is also due to change in turgor in the cells of sepals of flowers.
Plasmolysis

We know that when a plant cell is surrounded by hypertonic solution, the water leaves the cell by osmosis. Water is lost first from the cytoplasm and then from the vacuole. Due to this outward movement of water, the cytoplasm shrinks and pulls away from the cell wall. This process is known as plasmolysis and the cell is said to be plasmolysed.
Plasmolysis
When a plasmolysed cell is placed in a hypotonic solution, the cell restores its turgidity. The process is called deplasmolysis.
iv. Active Transport

Sometimes, cell membrane helps to move the substances against concentration gradient i.e. from an area of lower concentration to the area of higher concentration. This uphill movement requires the expenditure of energy (ATP) and is called active transport. For the active transport of substances, carrier proteins present in cell membrane use energy and move them against the concentration gradient.
iv. Active Transport

Na⁺/K⁺ are actively transported across the membrane according to the requirement of the cell/body. For example, nerve impulse is carried when Na⁺ is actively transported across the membrane from nerve cell to outside.

v. Endocytosis and Exocytosis

Endocytosis is a general term for the process that brings macromolecules, large particles and even small cells into the cell. In endocytosis, the cell membrane invaginates (folds inward) and takes in the materials from the environment, forming a small pocket. The pocket deepens, forming a vesicle. This vesicle separates from the plasma membrane and migrates with its contents to the cell's interior.
Scientific Information
There are two forms of endocytosis i.e. phagocytosis (cellular eating) and pinocytosis (cellular drinking). In phagocytosis cell takes in solid material while in pinocytosis cell takes in liquid.
v. Endocytosis and Exocytosis

Exocytosis is the process by which materials packaged in vesicles are excreted from a cell. The initial event in this process is the binding of vesicle membrane with the cell membrane. Then, the contents of the vesicle are released to the environment and the vesicle membrane is incorporated into cell membrane.

4.7 Tissues

All plants and animals have tissues. Tissue is a group of cells which perform a common function. All cells of the tissues are dependent on each other. However, there are organisms where cells group together but they do not form tissues. This is because the cells are not dependent but function independently. Volvox is a common example of such organization (recall from Unit-1).
4.7 Tissues
In Volvox, many cells combine together forming a colony but they do not form tissues. Other examples of such organizations are bacteria, slime molds etc.
4.7 Tissues
There are various types of tissues in plants and animals depending upon their functions or morphology.
4.7.1 Plant Tissues
Plant tissues may be classified into two major groups i.e. simple tissues and compound tissues.
A. Simple Tissues
They are composed of only one type of cells. They are further classified into:
A. Simple Tissues
a. Meristematic Tissues or Embryonic Tissues
a. Meristematic Tissues or Embryonic Tissues

These are made up of those cells which have the ability to divide and produce new cells at the growing points of a plant. The cells of meristematic tissue have dense cytoplasm, a large central nucleus with small or no vacuoles. Cells are alike, with no intercellular spaces and have thin walls. These tissues are of two types:
a. Meristematic Tissues or Embryonic Tissues

Apical meristem is present at the apex of root and shoot. Here the cells of meristem divide and redivide and result in the elongation of stem and root. Such a growth is called primary growth. • Lateral meristem is present on the lateral sides of roots and shoot. Here, the cells divide and results in the increase of thickness of root and shoot. Such a growth is called secondary growth.
a. Meristematic Tissues or Embryonic Tissues
Figure 4.25: Apical and lateral meristem
b. Permanent Tissues
The cells of these tissues lack the ability to divide. They originate from the primary meristem. The permanent tissues consist of epidermal, ground, supporting or mechanical tissues.
Scientific Information

Plants have certain areas where meristematic tissues are present such as tips of root and shoot. These tips can be used for the proliferation of high quality plants through tissue culture especially where other vegetative methods fail to work.
Epidermal Tissues

These tissues are present as outermost protective covering of leaf, stem and root. Cells of the epidermal tissues are flattened and irregular in shape. They are thick walled and are closely packed with no intercellular spaces. In stem, the walls of these cells are covered with waxy material which prevents loss of water. In leaves, the epidermal tissue has small guarded openings called stomata, for gaseous exchange.
Scientific Information
The cells of root epidermal tissue also have extensions in the form of root hairs.
Ground Tissues

This tissue is present in all parts of the plant except the epidermal tissue and vascular tissue. It is composed of thin walled cells called parenchyma cells. These cells are oval, spherical or polygonal in shape. Their walls are thin. They store food. In leaves, the ground tissue contains chlorophyll and is called mesophyll tissue. It prepares food.
Ground Tissues

Supporting or Mechanical Tissues
Plants need support to maintain their shape and remain stable. Supporting tissues provide strength and flexibility to the plant. These are of two types:
Supporting or Mechanical Tissues
a. Collenchyma Tissue: It is found in young stems where it provides strength to different parts of the plant. The cells of this tissue are living, elongated and polygonal with tapering ends.
Supporting or Mechanical Tissues
b. Sclerenchyma Tissue: These are thick walled dead cells. Walls of these cells are heavily filled with lignin which provides hardness and strength to the cell.
B. Compound Tissues
These are the tissues which are composed of more than one type of cells performing a common function. Xylem and phloem tissues found in the vascular bundles are examples of compound tissues.
B. Compound Tissues

a. Xylem Tissue: Xylem tissue consists of two types of cells i.e. vessels and tracheids. Vessel cells are short and wide and have thick secondary cell walls. These cells are dead and hollow and join together to form long tubes. Tracheids are long, slender cells with overlapping ends. Water moves upward from tracheid to tracheid.
B. Compound Tissues

Xylem tissue is responsible for the transport of water and dissolved substances from roots to the upper parts. Due to the presence of lignin in the secondary walls of its cells, xylem tissue also provides support to the plant body.
B. Compound Tissues

b. Phloem Tissue: Phloem tissue consists of sieve tube cells and companion cells. In Sieve tube cells, protoplasm has no nucleus and the end walls have small pores called sieve plates. The transport of food occurs through the cytoplasm of the sieve tube cells. Companion cells accompany the sieve tube cells. They regulate the movement of food through sieve tubes.

4.8 Animal Tissues
Animal tissues are classified according to their structure and functions into four major types.
4.8 Animal Tissues
i. Epithelial tissues • ii. Connective tissues • iii. Muscular tissues • iv. Nervous tissues
i. Epithelial Tissues

The interior of the body is physically separated from the outside world by the skin. The skin is made of epithelial tissue, which is in the form of continuous sheets of cells. Epithelial tissue also lines the gut, lungs and urinary tract. Structurally these cells are flattened and elongated.
ii. Connective Tissue
Connective tissue is the major supporting tissue of the animal body. Its cells are scattered through an extracellular material. There are many types of connective tissues.
ii. Connective Tissue

a. Loose Connective Tissue: Its extracellular material contains loosely packed collagen (a protein) fibers. It is widely distributed under the epithelial tissues. It holds organs at their specific place.
ii. Connective Tissue
b. Fibrous Connective Tissue: Its extracellular material contains tightly packed collagen fibers. It is in the form of tendons which attach muscles to bones and ligaments join two bones.
ii. Connective Tissue

c. Adipose Tissue: It contains swollen cells due to the presence of large number of fat droplets. It is found around kidneys, under skin, in abdomen etc. It provides energy, insulates against heat loss and protects and supports organs.
ii. Connective Tissue

d. Cartilage: Its extracellular material contains bundles of collagen fibers and rubbery substance. It is found around the ends of bones, in external ear, in nose, trachea and larynx etc. It provides support and maintains shape while allowing flexibility.
ii. Connective Tissue
e. Bone: Its extracellular material contains collagen fibers and calcium salts. It supports, protects, provide lever system for movements, stores calcium and forms blood cells.
ii. Connective Tissue

f. Blood: It is a special type of connective tissue. Its extracellular material (plasma) is fluid. It transports substances from one part of the body to the other and is also responsible for immunity.
iii. Muscular Tissue

It consist of highly specialized contractile cells or fibers held together by connective tissue. Each muscle fiber is an elongated cell which has the ability to contract and relax. Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscles are the examples of these tissues.
iii. Muscular Tissue

a. Skeletal muscles: These are attached to cartilages and bones with the help of connective tissues called tendons. They are composed of striated (striped) cells that are long and cylindrical. The cells of skeletal muscles contain many nuclei. Skeletal muscles are voluntary and produce powerful, rapid contractions. It helps arms and legs to move.
iii. Muscular Tissue

b. Smooth muscles: These are found in the walls of hollow structures such as blood vessels, gut etc. They produce slow contractions. Their contraction moves substances (foodstuff, urine) in the hollow organs. They are composed of Spindle shaped, un-striated muscles and are involuntary in action.
iii. Muscular Tissue

c. Cardiac muscle: These are found in heart. These are composed of branched fibers and are capable of sustained contraction. Their contraction produces heartbeat that propels blood into vessels. They are also involuntary in action.
iv. Nervous Tissue

It is composed of nerve cells which are called neurons. Neurons are capable of transmitting nerve impulses to conduct messages in the whole body. Nervous tissue is found in brain, spinal cord and nerves.

5.1 Cell Cycle and Interphase

Recall cell theory. A key element of cell theory is, "all cells arise from pre-existing cells by cell division". Cells division is an important character of cells. All cells divide to produce new ones. In this unit, you will study cell division and its types.
Cell Cycle

In living organisms, many processes like growth, reproduction, repairing and healing are dependent on cell division. When a cell divides, it produces daughter cells. The daughter cells grow in size and begin to perform their functions. After maturity, daughter cells divide again and produce their next generation.
Cell Cycle
The series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell leading to its replication is called cell cycle. The cell cycle consists of two main stages:
Cell Cycle
Interphase or resting stage • Division phase (Mitosis or Meiosis)
5.1 Interphase or resting stage

The longest part of the cell cycle is the interphase stage. It is the period between the end of one cell division and the start of next division. In Interphase, the nucleolus and the nuclear envelope are distinct and the chromosomes are in the form of thread like chromatin.
5.1 Interphase or resting stage
Figure 5.1: A cell during interphase
Events of Interphase
Interphase may be divided into three sub phases. The following events occur during interphase.
Scientific Information
The S-phase and G2-phase are shorter than the G1. The duration of G1-phase may extend from a few hours to several days, depending on the type of cell.
Events of Interphase

i) G1-phase: G1-phase (G stands for gap) is the first and the longest sub-phase of the interphase. In this phase, newly produced cells grow in size and undergo internal chemical changes, which prepare the daughter cells for DNA replication. During G1-phase RNA, ribosome and several enzymes are synthesized.
Events of Interphase

ii) S-phase (synthesis phase): In this phase, the cell duplicates its chromosomes. For this purpose, the DNA molecule of each chromosome is copied (replication of DNA) and new protein molecules are attached. Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids. Cell growth continues throughout S phase. At the same time, synthesis of proteins and enzymes take place which are involved in DNA synthesis.
G0 phase

Many cells stop dividing temporarily or permanently and continue to do their specialized jobs. This phase in cell cycle is called G0 phase. Many cells (e.g. neurons) remain in G0 for indefinite period of time. Some cell (e.g. cells of the liver and kidney) enter the G0 phase semi-permanently. They can again start dividing under specific conditions. Some cells (e.g.
G0 phase
epithelial cells) do not enter G0 and continue to divide throughout life.
Events of Interphase

iii. G2-phase: It is the period between completion of DNA synthesis and the beginning of active cell division phase. During G2-phase, cell prepares proteins e.g. microtubule framework (spindle fibres) required for cell division.
Events of Interphase

A final event in interphase occurs with the replication of the centrioles and their movement to either end of the nucleus. At the same time, microtubules appear radiating from the area of centriole at each end.
5.2 Division Phase: Mitosis
During the division phase, the cell undergoes division either by Mitosis or Meiosis.
Scientific Information
Mitosis takes place in eukaryotic cells. Whereas, in prokaryotic cells binary fission takes place which is called amitosis
5.2.1 Mitosis

A German biologist named Walther Flemming observed a dividing cell. He noticed that during division, nucleus passes through a series of changes. He called these changes as mitosis. In this type of cell division, the cell divides into two daughter cells. In each daughter cell, the chromosome number is maintained at the same level as that in the parent cell.
Point to Ponder
The prokaryotes do not undergo mitosis. Why?
Stages of mitosis
For convenience, the process of mitosis can be divided into two main stages.
Stages of mitosis
A. Karyokinesis: It is the division of the nucleus. "Karyo" means nucleus and "kinesis" means division
Stages of mitosis
B. Cytokinesis: It is the division of cytoplasm.
Scientific Information
During S phase of interphase, the parent cell makes a copy of each chromosome. In mitosis, the copies of chromosomes are distributed equally to both daughter cells.
Stages of mitosis
Karyokinesis: It is further divided into four phases i.e. prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
i. Prophase
Chromatin threads condense, coil and shorten to become chromosomes. Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids attached at the centromere. The chromosomes are now visible under a microscope.
i. Prophase

In an animal cell, the two pairs of centrioles reach opposite poles of the cell. They make a network of spindle fibres between the two poles. The complete set of spindle fibres is called mitotic apparatus. In plant cells, there are no centrioles. Their mitotic spindle is formed by the aggregation of spindle fibres present in cytoplasm.
i. Prophase
As a part of the changes of prophase, the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
ii. Metaphase

In metaphase, some spindle fibres attach with chromosomes. Two spindle fibres from both sides attach with one chromosome. The chromosomes attached with spindle fibres arrange themselves at the equator of the cell. In this way a plate is formed called metaphase plate.
iii. Anaphase
The centromere of each chromosome splits. The spindle fibres pull the chromatids apart to opposite poles. Once the chromatids are separated, they are called daughter chromosomes.
iii. Anaphase
In early anaphase the centromere split. Half the chromosomes move to one pole and half to the other pole.
iii. Anaphase
In late anaphase the chromosomes have almost reached their respective poles. The cell membrane begins to move inward at the centre.
iv. Telophase

In telophase, spindle fibres break down. A nuclear envelope forms around the chromosomes at each pole of the cell. Thus two daughter nuclei are formed, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent nucleus.
iv. Telophase
A nucleolus forms and the chromosomes uncoil to become thin chromatin network.
B. Cytokinesis

After the division of nucleus, the cytoplasm divides. The division of cytoplasm is called cytokinesis. In animal cells, cleavage or furrows appear in the cytoplasm between the two nuclei. The furrows deepen and two identical daughter cells are finally produced.
B. Cytokinesis

In plant cells, a cell plate is formed between the two daughter nuclei. It divides the cell into two. The cell plate is formed by the fusion of small fluid-filled vesicles produced by the Golgi apparatus.
B. Cytokinesis
Cytokinesis in plant cell
Significance of Mitosis
Mitosis plays the following significant roles in the life of an organism.
Significance of Mitosis
a. Growth: For a multicellular organism to grow, new cells are produced by mitosis.
Significance of Mitosis

b. Repair of worn-out parts: Each time you brush your teeth and rinse your mouth, hundreds of dead and worn-out cheek cells are being shed into your saliva. These dead cells are constantly being replaced by the process of mitosis.
Significance of Mitosis

c. Asexual reproduction: Many organisms reproduce asexually. For example, cutting, grafting, budding etc. Hydra reproduces asexually by budding. During this process, mitosis forms a mass of cells called bud on the surface of Hydra. The mitosis continues in the cells of the bud and it grows into a new Hydra.
Significance of Mitosis
Flowering plants are capable of vegetative reproduction through the process of mitosis in their vegetative parts i.e. shoots and roots.
Significance of Mitosis

d. Regeneration: It is the process of the renewal of organisms or the worn-out cells and tissues. All organisms have the ability to regenerate cells and tissues that are broken due to certain processes such as necrosis etc, for example regeneration of tail in lizards. Other organisms have the ability to regenerate the whole body from a piece of the body, e.g. hydra.

Meiosis

Meiosis was discovered in 1876, by a German biologist Oscar Hertwig. Meiosis is the type of cell division, in which each daughter cell receives half the number of chromosomes as the parent cell. It is also called reduction division as the diploid number of chromosomes (2n) is reduced to haploid (n). As a result of meiosis a single diploid cell gives rise to four haploid cells. Meiosis is divided into two stages i.e.

Scientific Information
In parent cell, the chromosomes are in the form of homologous pairs. This paired number of chromosomes is called diploid (2n).
Scientific Information
When chromosomes are not in pairs, their number is called haploid (n).
A. Meiosis-I
This phase comprises of the following stages;
Scientific Information
In meiosis I, the diploid homologous chromosomes in parent cell separate to produce haploid sets of chromosomes in the daughter cells.
i) Prophase-1

Prophase - 1 usually accounts for 90% of the total time spent in meiosis. In this phase, the chromatin material condenses and chromosomes become visible. However, unlike prophase of mitosis, the two homologous chromosomes (chromosome similar in shape and size) pair up or synapse to form tetrads (because a pair of chromosome has four chromatids).
i) Prophase-1

The two non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes become zipped together, forming complexes known as chiasmata (singular chiasma). At chiasma, the non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange their parts. This process is known as crossing over. As in the prophase of mitosis, here also the nucleoli disappear and nuclear envelope breaks. Centrioles migrate to opposite poles and make spindle fibres.
i) Prophase-1
Figure 5.3: Showing different events of Chiasma formation during crossing over
ii) Metaphase-1

Homologous chromosomes arrange themselves during the metaphase plate. Spindle fibres from one pole attaches to one chromosomes of each homologous pair while spindle fibres from the opposite pole attach to the other chromosome of the homologous pair.
iii) Anaphase-I

During anaphase-I, spindle fibres pull towards the poles and separate the homologous chromosomes. Each member of the pair is pulled toward opposite poles of the cell. During this phase, the sister chromatids remain attached. In this way, one haploid set of chromosomes is formed at each pole. Each chromosome in both haploid sets still contains two sister chromatids.
Scientific Information

Anaphase-I is a key event in creating new genetic combinations in sexually reproducing organisms. New combinations of genetic material created by any process including crossing-over, is termed as genetic recombination.
iv) Telophase-I
After the chromosomes reach their respective poles, the nuclear membrane reappears along with the appearance of nucleoli. Later cytokinesis occurs and two haploid daughter cells are produced.
iv) Telophase-I

B. Meiosis-II

Each of the two cells formed in meiosis-I undergoes meiosis-II. Generally meiosis-II resembles mitosis, where simply the separation of chromatids takes place. However it differs from mitosis in that, parent cells have haploid numbers of chromosomes and the daughter cells also receive haploid number. Meiosis-II consists of Prophase-II, Metaphase-II, Anaphase-II and Telophase-II.
B. Meiosis-II

i) Prophase-II: The chromosomes become visible. Each chromosome comprises of a centromere and two chromatids. The Nucleoli and nuclear envelope disappear. Centrioles move to opposite poles and make spindle fibres.
B. Meiosis-II
ii) Metaphase-II: Chromosomes attach with spindle fibres and arrange themselves on the equator forming an equatorial plate.
B. Meiosis-II
iii) Anaphase-II: The centromere of each chromosome divides, due to the pull exerted by spindle fibres. Thus the sister chromatids of each chromosome move to the opposite pole.
B. Meiosis-II

iv) Telophase-II: The sister chromatids of each chromosome reach to the opposite poles. The nucleoli and nuclear membrane reappear. The cytoplasm then divides to form four haploid daughter cells from the two cells entering Meiosis.
Scientific Information
Mitosis usually occurs in the somatic cells (body cells) and results in growth, healing of wounds etc. while Meiosis occur is germs cells during the process of sexual reproduction

Significance of Meiosis
i) Formation of Gametes for sexual reproduction: Meiosis is essential for sexual reproduction.
Significance of Meiosis

In animals, the parent cells with diploid number of chromosomes undergo meiosis to produce haploid gametes, sperms in males and ova in females. The male and female gametes fuse together and make a zygote with diploid number. The zygote undergoes mitosis many times and develops into the new diploid organism.
Significance of Meiosis

In diploid plants, the spore-mother cells (with diploid number of chromosomes) undergo meiosis to make haploid spores. These spores grow into haploid structures which produce haploid gametes by mitosis. The gametes combine to produce the diploid zygote. The zygote undergoes repeated mitosis to become the new diploid plants.
Scientific Information

Many organisms are haploid (e.g. fungi and many unicellular protists). They make haploid gametes by mitosis. When gametes fuse, diploid zygote is formed. The diploid zygote undergoes meiosis and makes four haploid cells. These cells undergo mitosis to create the haploid organism again.
ii) Genetic Variations during sexual reproduction:

Meiosis helps to create genetic variations among the offspring. During meiosis, the chromosomes of each parent undergo genetic recombination. It produces gametes with different genetic combinations. Gametes fuse to from zygote with different genetic combination.
ii) Genetic Variations during sexual reproduction:
Thus meiosis allows a species to bring variations to handle the changes in the environment.

Apoptosis

Apoptosis is sometimes called programmed cell death. It is a way to remove unwanted cells. During apoptosis, cellular contents are not released and inflammation does not occur. The apoptotic cells are rapidly engulfed by their neighbours and removed. Programmed cell death is a normal and necessary event of normal development.
Examples:
i) During metamorphosis, the tail of tadpole disappears by apoptosis.
Examples:
ii) During human development, the web present between fingers disappears by apoptosis.
Examples:
iii) In the adult organisms, the number of cells is kept relatively constant through apoptosis and division.

Human growth and development are dependent on cell division. However, the uncontrolled cell division may lead to the tumours formation in the tissues. Tumours may be cancerous or noncancerous. Nevertheless, the mature cells, for example the nerve cells, use their energies and resources in the functions for which they are specialised, therefore they do not divide.
Necrosis

Necrosis is the death of most or all of the cells in an organ or tissue due to diseases, injury or failure of the blood supply. A number of toxic chemicals or physical events like exposure to toxins, radiation, heat, trauma, lack of oxygen due to the blockage of blood flow etc. Can cause necrosis.
Necrosis
As necrotic cells begin to die, they swell up and holes appear in the plasma membrane and intracellular materials spill out into the surrounding environment.

6.1 Metabolism

The characteristics of living things, such as breathing, growth, reproduction and responsiveness to stimuli are the outcome of chemical reactions taking place inside the body of a living organism. The chemical processes that occur within a living organism in order to maintain life are collectively called metabolism. All these reactions are controlled by specific proteins called enzymes.
6.1 Metabolism
In this unit, we will study enzymes and how they control metabolism.
6.1 Metabolism

The sum of all chemical reactions going on within a living organism is called metabolism. Metabolism consists of anabolism and catabolism. Anabolism is building up of larger molecules from smaller ones. These type of reactions are known as anabolic reactions. Photosynthesis, is a process by which smaller and simpler molecules (water and carbon dioxide) react to form a larger and complex molecule (glucose).
6.1 Metabolism

Therefore, it is an example of anabolism. Whereas, catabolism is the breakdown of larger molecules into smaller ones. These type of reactions are known as catabolic reactions. In respiration, a larger and complex molecule (glucose) is broken down into smaller and simpler molecules (carbon dioxide and water). Therefore, it is an example of catabolism.

6.1 Metabolism

Enzymes are biological catalysts which speed up the chemical reactions within the body, without getting consumed. The molecules that react in the enzyme-catalysed reactions are called substrates and the molecules produced in the reactions are called products.
Point to remember
The term "enzyme" was first of all used by a German physiologist Winhelm Kuhne in 1878. Enzymes kick start biochemical reactions
6.2 Enzymes lower the Activation Energy

Whenever a chemical reaction takes place some amount of energy is spent to break the chemical bonds in reactants (substrates). This energy is called activation energy. Enzymes lower off the amount of activation energy. Thus, in the presence of enzymes, reactions proceed at a faster rate. Enzymes act in many ways to lower the activation energy.
6.2 Enzymes lower the Activation Energy
For example; they change the shape of substrate molecules or bring them in correct orientation. They may also disrupt the charge distribution on substrate molecules.
Point to remember

Complex apparatus and high temperatures are required to break down carbohydrates, fats or proteins in the laboratory. However, with the help of enzymes, cells can carry out these reactions quite rapidly within normal body temperature.

6.3 Characteristics of Enzymes
i) Enzymes are proteins in nature and are secreted by cells.
6.3 Characteristics of Enzymes
ii) Enzymes function as catalysts and increase the rate of chemical reactions. They do so by lowering the activation energy.
6.3 Characteristics of Enzymes
iii) Enzymes are specific in action. They are specific not only for substrate but also for the kind of reaction.
6.3 Characteristics of Enzymes
iv) A small amount of an enzyme is needed to catalyze relatively large quantities of substrate. They are not used during the chemical reactions.
Point to remember

Enzymes are also classified according to the chemical reactions they catalyse. For example; the enzymes which catalyse hydrolysis (reactions in which water molecules are needed to break down complex molecule) are known as hydrolases.

v) All enzymes are synthesized inside the cells. Some enzymes work inside the cells and are called 'Intracellular enzymes' e.g. mitochondrial enzymes. Some enzymes are released from the cell and they work outside. Such enzymes are called extracellular enzymes e.g. pepsin enzyme working in the stomach cavity.
Scientific Information
Enzymes inhibitors are molecules that interact with enzyme to prevent it from working. Poisons and drugs are the examples of enzyme inhibitors.

vi) In complex metabolic reactions, many enzymes work together in a sequence. One enzyme takes the product of another enzyme as a substrate. After speeding up the reaction, the new product is passed on to another enzyme.

Specificity of Enzyme

We have studied that enzymes are specific for their substrate and the type of reaction. For example, the enzyme protease speed up the digestion of protein only. It does not catalyse the digestion of starch. Enzyme amylase works for the digestion of starch only. Similarly, enzyme cellulase speed up the digestion of cellulose only. Similarly, lipase digests lipids only.
Specificity of Enzyme
The specificity of different enzymes is due to the shape of their active sites. The active sites of each enzyme possess specific shape that fits with specific substrate.

6.4 Mechanism of Enzyme Action

There is a small portion in the enzyme molecule that is actually involved in catalysis. It is in the form of a depression or "pocket" on the surface of enzyme molecule. This catalytic region is called active site.
6.4 Mechanism of Enzyme Action

When an enzyme attaches with the substrate, a temporary enzyme-substrate (ES) complex is formed. The active site catalyzes the reaction and substrate is converted to product. The ES complex breaks and the enzyme and the product are released.
6.4 Mechanism of Enzyme Action
Enzyme (active site) + Substrate → Enzyme-Substrate (Complex) → Enzyme + Products
6.4 Mechanism of Enzyme Action
Two models have been proposed to explain the mechanism of enzyme action. These are the "lock and key model" and the "Induced fit model"
Lock and Key Model

This model was proposed by a German chemist Emil Fischer in 1894. According to this model, the active site of enzyme and the substrate have specific geometric shapes. The substrate molecule exactly fits in the active site of enzyme just like a lock and a key (enzyme is the lock and substrate is the key). This model suggests that the active site is a rigid and non-flexible structure.
Lock and Key Model
Figure 6.4: Lock and Key Model of enzyme action
Science, Technology and Society

There is a famous expression, "without which there is none" and this expression is very much true for the role of enzymes inside our body. Digestion could not be done without enzymes. We have foods that contain enzymes for their own digestion and we should prefer such foods. These food containing enzymes lower the burden of digestion on our digestive system.
Induced Fit Model:

Recent studies do not support lock and key model. On the basis of new evidences, in 1958 an American biologist Daniel Koshland proposed "Induced Fit Model". According to this model, when a substrate molecule fits in the active site of enzyme, the enzyme molecule alters the shape of active site slightly so that it fits more tightly around the substrate molecule (induced fit)

6.5 Factors that affect the rate of enzyme action
There are different factors which affect the enzyme activity. Some of them are discussed as follow.
a. Effect of Temperature on Enzyme Activity

Increase in temperature, speeds up the rate of enzyme catalyzed reactions but only to a point. Each enzyme works at the maximum rate at a specific temperature, which is called its optimum temperature. The optimum temperature of enzymes varies in different organisms. For most enzymes, the optimum temperature is about 40 - 45°C. Certain enzymes in plants have a high optimum temperature.
a. Effect of Temperature on Enzyme Activity
Decrease in temperature lowers the rate of reaction.
a. Effect of Temperature on Enzyme Activity

When temperature rises above the optimum temperature, the rate of reaction decreases rapidly. This is due to the denaturation (alteration in the structure) of the protein of enzyme. The average temperature of human body is 37°C. It is the optimum temperature for human enzymes. Human enzymes start to denature quickly at temperatures above 40°C.

b. Effect of pH on Enzyme Activity

Enzymes are affected by the acidity or alkalinity of the solutions in which they act. Each enzymes works best at a specific pH, which is called its optimum pH. Some work best in slightly acidic pH while others require slightly alkaline pH. Most enzymes function between a pH of 6 – 8, however pepsin in the stomach works best at a pH of 2 and trypsin at a pH of 8.
b. Effect of pH on Enzyme Activity
Any change in pH can lower the enzymatic activity. Extreme changes in the pH of solutions denature the enzymes.

c. Effect of Concentration of Substrate on Enzyme Activity

As the concentration of substrate increases, the rate of reaction increases. This is due to successful collisions with enzyme molecules. However, if the substrate concentration is increased beyond a saturation point, the active sites of enzyme are not available and rate of reaction does not increase more.

Key Points

Enzymes are biological or organic catalysts. They are made of proteins and can speed up the rate of chemical reactions without themselves being chemically changed at the end of the reactions. • Enzymes are specific in their actions because of the shape of their active sites. Only substances with shapes complementary to that of active site can fit into the enzyme molecules and be acted upon by the enzymes.
Key Points

• Factors affecting the rate of enzyme catalyzed reactions are temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration. • Every enzyme has its optimum temperature and pH. At optimum temperature and pH, an enzyme works at the greatest speed. • When temperature rises well above the optimum temperature, the protein structure of enzyme is denatured and so the rate of reaction decreases rapidly.
Key Points

• Enzymes are specific in action. They are specific not only for substrate but also for the kind of reaction. • Intracellular enzymes e.g. mitochondrial enzymes work inside the cells while extracellular enzymes e.g. pepsin are released from the cell and they work outside the cell. • Cofactors are the non-protein molecules required by enzymes for their action.
Key Points

• The cofactors called prosthetic groups make permanent attachment with the enzyme while the cofactors called coenzymes are not permanently attached to the enzyme. • An enzyme attaches with the substrate to form enzyme-substrate (ES) complex. The active site of enzyme catalyzes the reaction and substrate is converted to product.
Key Points

• The lock and key model of enzyme action states that the substrate molecule exactly fits in the active site of enzyme which is a rigid and non-flexible structure. • The induced fit model suggests that the enzyme molecule alters the shape of active site slightly so that it fits more tightly around the substrate molecule.

7.1 Bioenergetics

In previous unit, you have learnt about many activities that living organisms perform. These include cell division, respiration, growth, irritability etc. All these activities are possible because of chemical reactions occurring in their bodies (metabolism). Some reactions require energy while other reactions release energy. Organisms have very sophisticated systems of capturing, storing and utilizing energy.
7.1 Bioenergetics
In this unit, you will study the nature of energy used by organisms and the basic processes by which organisms capture and store energy.
7.1 Bioenergetics
Bioenergetics is the study of transformation of energy in organisms. All organisms need energy to keep them alive and functioning.
Scientific Information

The metabolic processes which occur inside the living bodies all the times, involve the making or breaking of bonds in the molecules. When chemical bonds are broken, energy is released and when bonds are formed, energy is stored.
7.1 Bioenergetics

Sun is the ultimate source of energy for all organisms. However, only autotrophs use this energy directly. They capture solar energy and convert it into stored chemical energy through the process of photosynthesis. The energy stored in food is then transformed into mechanical and heat energy during respiration. Thus, the two main processes involving energy transformation are photosynthesis and respiration.
7.1.1 Importance of Oxidation-Reduction Reactions

Both photosynthesis and respiration are basically oxidation-reduction processes. Oxidation is defined as the loss of hydrogen or electrons. Reduction is the opposite of oxidation in which hydrogen or electrons are gained.
Scientific Information
Energy can neither be stored nor released without oxidation-reduction reactions. Therefore, life processes would be impossible without oxidation-reduction reactions.
7.1.1 Importance of Oxidation-Reduction Reactions

In photosynthesis, a chain of oxidation-reduction reactions occurs during which carbon dioxide and water are combined to make food molecules. In these oxidation-reduction reactions, energy is stored in food molecules. Respiration is also oxidation-reduction process during which food molecules are broken down into carbon dioxide and water.
7.1.1 Importance of Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
In these oxidation-reduction reactions, energy is liberated from food molecules.

7.1.2 ATP as the Energy Currency of Cells

Cells use energy for performing activities like synthesis of proteins, cell division and growth etc. Energy is provided to all living cells by Adenosine Tri Phosphate (ATP). It is an energy rich molecule and is called as the "energy currency" of cells. Cells make ATPs to store energy while they break ATPs to get energy.

ATP molecule has 3 components i.e. one adenine (a nitrogenous base), one ribose sugar and three phosphate groups. The covalent bonds between phosphates groups are high-energy bonds.
Scientific Information
ATP is the currency of energy of a cell. A cell with more ATP is able to do more work.
7.1.2 ATP as the Energy Currency of Cells

When a cell needs energy, one bond between phosphate groups is broken. It releases 7.3 kcal (7,300 calories) energy. As a result, one inorganic phosphate (Pi) separates and ATP is converted to ADP (Adenosine Diphosphate).

7.1.2 ATP as the Energy Currency of Cells

ATP molecules are constantly broken by the cell into ADP and inorganic phosphate and energy is obtained. At the same time, ATP molecules are constantly regenerated from ADP and phosphate using energy released from the breakdown of food. This is how constant cycle of ATP breakdown and reformation goes on in the living cells.

7.2 Photosynthesis: A life sustaining process

The word Photosynthesis is the combination of two Greek words; "Photo" means light and "Synthesis" means to manufacture. Photosynthesis is defined as the manufacturing of organic food (glucose) in the presence of chlorophyll, using CO₂, water and sunlight and releasing oxygen as a byproduct. Photosynthesis occurs in autotrophic organisms (plants, algae, and some bacteria).
Science, Technology and Society

What do the photovoltaic array (solar energy system) and the tomato plant have in common? They both convert sunlight (radiant energy) into forms useful to humans. The photovoltaic array absorbs solar energy and stores it as chemical potential energy in batteries. The leaves of the tomato plant absorb solar energy that is (mainly) stored as chemical potential energy in compounds called carbohydrates

7.2 Photosynthesis: A life sustaining process
Carbon Dioxide + Water —(Sun light, Chlorophyll)→ Glucose + Oxygen + Water
7.2 Photosynthesis: A life sustaining process

Photosynthesis acts as energy capturing and storing process. Heterotrophic organisms cannot carry out photosynthesis and are unable to use energy of sunlight directly. Therefore, for their energy needs, they depend directly or indirectly on plants. Photosynthesis also provides oxygen, which is used by all aerobic organisms for respiration.
7.2.1 Role of Chlorophyll and Sunlight in photosynthesis

Chlorophyll is a complex organic compound. It absorbs sunlight (blue and red portion) and converts it into chemical energy for the formation of carbohydrates (glucose). The green portion of sunlight is mainly reflected. That is why chlorophyll appears green. When chlorophyll absorbs light, its electrons are excited. The energy of excited electrons is used to make ATP.
7.2.1 Role of Chlorophyll and Sunlight in photosynthesis
In plants and algae, chlorophyll is present in chloroplasts while in photosynthetic prokaryotes, it is present in the cell membrane.
7.2.1 Role of Chlorophyll and Sunlight in photosynthesis
Fig. 7.5: Chloroplast structure
Point to Ponder
Suggest what would happen to the living organisms if the process of photosynthesis stops.
Scientific Information
Photosynthetic prokaryotes lack chloroplasts but they do have unstacked photosynthetic membrances, which work like thylakoid membrane. Chlorophyll is attached to the thylakoid membrane.
7.2.1 Role of Chlorophyll and Sunlight in photosynthesis

The photosynthetic pigments are organized in the form of clusters, called photosystems, in thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. Chlorophyll-a is the main photosynthetic pigment. Others are called accessory pigments and include chlorophyll-b and carotenoids.
7.2.1 Role of Chlorophyll and Sunlight in photosynthesis
Chlorophylls absorb mainly blue and red lights. Some wave lengths are not absorbed by chlorophyll -a and are very affectively absorbed by accessory pigments and vice-versa.
7.2.2 Intake of Carbon dioxide and Water by Plants

CO₂ is present in air and it is one of the raw materials for photosynthesis. CO₂ is diffused from the outside air into the intercellular spaces of leaf through stomata. Stomata are small openings scattered particularly in the lower epidermis of leaf. Each stoma is guarded by two kidney shaped guard cells.
7.2.2 Intake of Carbon dioxide and Water by Plants

Opening and closing of stomata regulates the diffusion of CO₂, water vapours and O₂ between the intercellular spaces of leaf mesophyll and the external air. After diffusing into the intercellular spaces, CO₂ attaches to the wet surfaces of mesophyll cells. Then it diffuses into the green cells and enters the stroma of chloroplasts.
7.2.2 Intake of Carbon dioxide and Water by Plants
In the dark reaction of photosynthesis, CO₂ molecules are reduced to form glucose molecules.
7.2.2 Intake of Carbon dioxide and Water by Plants

Water is also an essential requirement of photosynthesis. Water is absorbed by the roots of plants from the soil. It is then transported upward to the stem and leaves through xylem vessels. Most of this water is transpired from the leaves while a small portion is used in photosynthesis.
Scientific Information
Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) is a coenzyme. Its reduced form is NADH. One form of this coenzyme also carries phosphate with it and is therefore called NADP.
7.2.3 Mechanism of Photosynthesis
The process of photosynthesis is completed in two steps.
i) Light Reactions

Light reactions take place in the granum of chloroplast. Chlorophyll molecules absorb light. Their energy level increases and their excited electrons are released. These high energy electrons are used to produce ATP from ADP and Pi. Light also breaks water molecule into hydrogen and oxygen (O₂). Oxygen is released while hydrogen atoms are used to reduce NADP into NADPH.
i) Light Reactions

ii) Dark Reactions (Calvin Cycle)

The details of dark reactions were discovered by Melvin Calvin. Dark reactions occur in the stroma of chloroplast. These reactions do not require energy of sunlight. During dark reactions, CO₂ molecules are reduced to make carbohydrates. For the reduction of CO₂, ATP provides energy while NADPH provides hydrogen.
ii) Dark Reactions (Calvin Cycle)

Science, Technology and Society

Green plants are the primary producers as they are responsible for trapping light. Ultimately, this energy then travels to all other organism. We can improve the light trapping by adopting strategies at the producer level. Evergreen plants and broad leaved plants could increase the absorption of light and could ultimately be the sources of energy for the heterotrophs.
7.3 The Concept of Limiting Factors in Photosynthesis

Any environmental factors absence or deficiency of which can decrease the rate of a metabolic reaction, is called limiting factor for that reaction. Many factors act as the limiting factors for photosynthesis. Important limiting factors of photosynthesis are light intensity, temperature, concentration of carbon dioxide and the availability of water.
i) Effect of Light Intensity
Light is a form of radiant energy which the chlorophyll absorbs and converts into chemical energy. This chemical energy is stored in organic compounds.
Quranic Information
Allah, the Almighty has created sun as the ultimate source of energy (food) which sustains all life forms on earth.
i) Effect of Light Intensity
Light intensity and quality varies from place to place and time to time. At dawn and sunset and in winter the intensity of light is low. The intensity of light is maximum at midday.
i) Effect of Light Intensity

The quality and intensity of light affects the rate of photosynthesis. Very intense light damages chlorophyll and therefore has indirect effect on the rate of photosynthesis. Very weak light has low energy and therefore energy absorption by the chlorophyll is low. This results in lower rate of photosynthesis.
ii) Effect of CO₂ Concentration

Carbon dioxide is one of the raw materials for photosynthesis. It provides carbon for the synthesis of glucose. As carbon dioxide concentrations rise, the rate of dark reaction increases. Various factors affect the closing and opening of stomata. When stomata are closed, the concentration of CO₂ falls down in the mesophyll tissue. This lowers down the rate of photosynthesis.
Scientific Information

Carbon dioxide is almost 0.03 percent in air. It is constantly removed from air by the autotrophs and is used in photosynthesis. This concentration of CO₂ almost remains constant in air because it is produced in respiration by all living organisms.
iii. Effect of Temperature

An optimum temperature is necessary for normal process of photosynthesis. Increase and decrease in temperature negatively affects the rate of photosynthesis. Generally a temperature, ranging between 20°C and 30°C is most suitable for photosynthesis. When temperature exceeds 30°C, the rate of photosynthesis lowers down. Similarly, at low temperature the rate declines and at freezing temperature it stops completely.
iii. Effect of Temperature
However, plants growing in dry and hot localities and in cold regions have developed adaptations for high and low temperatures.

7.4 Respiration

Respiration is defined as oxidation-reduction processes which occur inside the living cells during which organic food is broken down into carbon dioxide and water and energy is released. Glucose is the most common food used in this process. The purpose of respiration is to release energy for the living processes. Respiration is common to all living organisms because all of them need energy for life activities.
Scientific Information

The term "cellular respiration" is used for the oxidation-reduction of food inside the cells. While the term "external respiration" or "breathing" means the exchange of respiratory gases (CO₂ and O₂) between the organism and its environment.

7.4.1 Types of Respiration
Respiration is of two types: Anaerobic and Aerobic
a. Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration (Fermentation) occurs in the absence of oxygen. It involves incomplete breakdown of organic food molecules and only a small amount of energy is released. It occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell. Anaerobic respiration is of two types; lactic acid fermentation and alcoholic fermentation.
i) Lactic Acid Fermentation

Lactic Acid Fermentation occurs in many microorganisms and also in the muscle cells of human beings when more energy is needed. It completes in two steps. Glycolysis is the first step in which glucose is broken down into two molecules of pyruvic acid and NAD is reduced to NADH. In the next step, Pyruvic acid is reduced by NADH into lactic acid.
i) Lactic Acid Fermentation
In the process, only two ATP molecules are produced from one glucose molecule.
Scientific Information
Yoghurt is a dairy product produced by bacterial fermentation of milk. Fermentation of lactose produces lactic acid, which acts on milk protein to give yoghurt its texture and characteristic taste.
i) Lactic Acid Fermentation
Figure 7.9: Lactic acid Fermentation
ii) Alcoholic Fermentation

It occurs in yeast and some bacteria. This type of anaerobic respiration is also completed in two steps: First step is glycolysis during which a glucose molecule is broken down into two molecules of pyruvic acid and NAD is reduced to NADH. In the next step, pyruvic acid is reduced by NADH to ethyl alcohol and CO₂. In alcoholic fermentation also two ATP molecules are produced from one glucose molecule.
ii) Alcoholic Fermentation

Scientific Information

Yeast and some bacteria convert sugars into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide. During the fermentation process of bread, sugar is converted into alcohol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide will form bubbles, which will be trapped by the gluten of the wheat causing the bread to rise.
Scientific Information
Because the bread fermentation takes a short period, only small amounts of alcohol are formed, most of which will evaporate during the bread baking process.
Science, Technology and Society

The practices of biotechnology are old and the human beings have used them since early history. Some of such practices include fermentation. Peoples have used grapes, berries, corn, rice, wheat, honey, potatoes, barley and other plant materials for fermentation. Various forms of alcohol are made for different purposes.
b. Aerobic Respiration
Aerobic respiration needs free O₂. In aerobic respiration, organic food is completely broken down into CO₂ and H₂O and large amount of stored energy is released.
b. Aerobic Respiration
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + 36 ATP (net gain)
b. Aerobic Respiration
Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + 36 ATPs
b. Aerobic Respiration
Aerobic Respiration completes in three steps:
b. Aerobic Respiration
i. Glycolysis occurs in cytoplasm • ii. Krebs Cycle occurs in mitochondria • iii. Electron transport chain also occurs in mitochondria
i) Glycolysis

"Glyco" means glucose and "lysis" means splitting. Glycolysis is the breakdown of one glucose molecule (6 carbon compound) into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3 carbon compound). It takes place in the cytoplasm. In glycolysis, there is a net gain of two ATP molecules. Oxygen is not required for this process. That is why glycolysis occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
ii) Krebs Cycle
This was discovered by a British scientist, Sir Hans Krebs and therefore named after his name as Krebs Cycle. It occurs in mitochondria where all the necessary enzymes are present.
ii) Krebs Cycle

Before entering in Krebs cycle, pyruvic acids (generated in glycolysis) is changed into a 2-carbon compound called acetyl-Coenzyme A. It then goes through a series of reactions in which it is completely oxidised. These reactions produce CO₂ along with ATP. In these reactions, coenzymes NAD and FAD (Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide) are reduced to NADH and FADH₂ respectively.
iii) Electron Transport Chain

The last step in aerobic respiration is the oxidation of reduced coenzymes (NADH and FADH₂) produced in glycolysis and Krebs cycle. It is done by using oxygen. During this step, two electrons are released from NADH and FADH₂. These electrons then pass along a series of electron carriers called cytochromes. During the transport from one cytochrome to the other, electrons lose energy.
iii) Electron Transport Chain
This energy is used to form ATP from ADP and Pi. At the end, the oxygen molecules accept electrons to form water.
7.4.2 Energy Produced in Respiration

The complete oxidation of one molecule of glucose into CO₂ and water generates 38 ATP. During glycolysis, two ATP molecules are also used. So there is net gain of 36 ATP from one glucose molecule. These ATP are generated step wise, some during glycolysis, some during Krebs cycle and many are generated during the electron transport chain.

8.1 Mineral Nutrition in Plants

In previous unit, we studied that all organisms need energy to perform their functions. We also know that they get this energy by the oxidation of food. Heterotrophs obtain food from others. On the other hand, autotrophs make their own food by photosynthesis. For making their food, autotrophs need to take essential materials from their environment.
8.1 Mineral Nutrition in Plants

Nutrients are the materials (elements and compounds) that organisms obtain and use for maintaining life. The term "nutrition" means the processes in which organisms obtain essential materials for making food or take food made by others, and convert it into substances for growth, energy and regulating various body functions. In this unit, we will study what the nutritional requirements of plants are?
8.1 Mineral Nutrition in Plants
We will also study the components of human food and the process by which food is digested in human body.
8.1 Mineral Nutrition in Plants

Along with basic factors necessary for photosynthesis (CO₂, water, sunlight, chlorophyll etc.), plants also need many mineral nutrients. Soil is the store house of these minerals. The processes which deal with how plants get minerals and where they use them, is called mineral nutrition in plants.
8.1 Mineral Nutrition in Plants

We can classify nutrients required as macronutrients and micronutrient on the basis of the quantity needed by the plant. The nutrients which are required in larger quantities are called macronutrients. These are nine in number. Similarly, the nutrients which are required in lower quantities are called micronutrients. These are eight in number.

8.1.1 Role of Nitrogen

You have noticed in table 8.1 that nitrogen is a major component of proteins, hormones, chlorophyll, vitamins and enzymes essential for plant life. Nitrogen metabolism is a major factor in stem and leaf growth. Too much nitrogen supply can delay flowering and fruit production. Deficiencies of nitrogen can reduce yields, cause yellowing of the leaves and stunted growth.
Point to remember
Proteins are made up of amino acids. Nitrogen is the key element of all amino acids. The chemical properties of the amino acids present in a protein determine the properties of that protein.
8.1.2 Role of Magnesium

Plants require Magnesium to form chlorophyll. It is the central part of chlorophyll Molecule. Without magnesium, plants would not be able to make chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. Deficiency of Magnesium in plants leads to chlorosis i.e. yellowing of leaves.
8.1.2 Role of Magnesium
Magnesium is also needed for the activation of many enzymes so its deficiency may affect normal rate of metabolism and ultimately lead to necrosis (cell death).
Scientific Information

Chlorosis is a condition in which leaves produce insufficient chlorophyll. Chlorotic leaves are pale, yellow, or yellow-white. The affected plant has little or no ability to make carbohydrates through photosynthesis. It may die unless the cause of its chlorophyll insufficiency is treated.

8.2 Importance of Fertilizers

You know that different nutrient materials play an important role in a plant's metabolic activities. Plants are directly affected by the quality and quantity of certain nutrient present in the soil. Most of the soils are deficient in nutrients that are required for optimum growth of plants. That is why, nutrients are added to the soil to get desired results e.g., more fruit, faster growth etc. in plants.
8.2 Importance of Fertilizers
Such nutrients are called fertilizers. Fertilizers are broadly classified into organic and inorganic.
Point to remember

Even if a land is fertile, crops absorb nutrients and leave the soil less fertile with the passage of time. By using fertilizers, we can ensure that soil provides proper amounts of nutrients to the growing plants.
8.2 Importance of Fertilizers

a. Organic Fertilizers are derived from plant or animal materials. Manure, compost and seaweed are good examples of organic fertilizers. Similarly, plant material called mulch e.g. hay, leaves, bark, wood chips, seed hulls and corn husks are also organic fertilizer.
8.2.1 Advantages of organic fertilizers

Improve the structure of the soil. • Retain soil moisture and increase aeration. • Release nutrients slowly and consistently • Less risk of leaching • Increase the ability of the soil to hold nutrients
8.2.1 Advantages of organic fertilizers

b. Inorganic or Chemical Fertilizers are primarily derived from chemical compounds such as ammonium nitrate, ammonium phosphate and potassium chloride. Examples of inorganic fertilizers are sodium nitrate, mined rock phosphate and limestone.
8.2.2 Advantages of inorganic fertilizers

Higher and accurate amount of nitrogen promotes protein and chlorophyll synthesis and encourages growth of stems and leaves. • Higher amount of phosphorus results in more flowers, larger fruits and healthier roots.
8.2.3 Environmental Hazards related to use of Chemical Fertilizers
The major risks to soil quality from chemical fertilizers are following.
8.2.3 Environmental Hazards related to use of Chemical Fertilizers

Increased soil salinity and acidity. • Storage and application of some nitrogen fertilizers may cause emissions of the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide. • The major risk to groundwater quality from nutrient application is NO₃⁻ leaching to groundwater sources. This can harm human and animal health. • The major risk to surface water is increased number of algae growing on the surface of water (eutrophication).

It is recommended that analysis of the nutrient content of the soil and nutrient requirements of the crop are done before the application of inorganic fertilizers.

Many human activities cause additional nutrients, such as phosphates and nitrates, to enter rivers and lakes, a process known as eutrophication. This promotes the growth of algae and other types of plankton thus depleting the oxygen in water bodies and making it difficult for aquatic organisms to survive.
8.3 Components of Human Food
Like all other organisms, human beings require food to grow, reproduce and maintain good health. The following are the major components of human food.
i. Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are the major source of energy. They contain the elements carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. We obtain most of our carbohydrate in the form of starch. This is found in potato, rice, bread and cereals. Our digestive system turns this starch into a simpler carbohydrate called glucose. Blood carries glucose to all cells, where it is used in respiration for energy.
i. Carbohydrates

If a gram of carbohydrate is fully oxidized it produces about four kilocalories of energy. The glucose which is not used by cells is converted into glycogen that is stored in the muscles and liver. The body's glycogen storage capacity is limited, so any unused glucose is converted to fat.
Point to remember
We also get some of our carbohydrate in the form of sucrose. This is the sugar which we put in our tea and coffee. Our digestive system breaks sucrose molecules into glucose and fructose.
ii. Proteins

Proteins are required for growth and repair. Proteins are made up of simple units called amino acids. There are over 20 different amino acids. An amino acid contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sometimes sulphur. Proteins are large molecules, so they cannot get directly into our blood. They are broken into amino acids by our digestive system. Cells can convert the amino acids back into proteins.
ii. Proteins
When amino acids are broken down, they release nitrogen in the form of ammonia. Liver converts ammonia into urea and kidneys remove this urea in the form of urine
Scientific Information

Proteins are essential components of the cytoplasm, membranes and organelles. They are also the major parts of muscles, ligaments and tendons. Many proteins act as enzymes. Proteins can also be used as a source of energy.
ii. Proteins

One gram of proteins contains four kilocalories of energy. Plant sources of proteins are beans, pulses, cereals and dry fruits, whereas, animal sources include cheese, milk, poultry, fish, mutton and beef.
iii. Fats (Lipids)
Fats belong to a group of organic compounds called lipids. They are made up of fatty acids and glycerol. They contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
iii. Fats (Lipids)

Fats serve both structural and metabolic functions. When the body has used up the carbohydrates, it oxidizes fats to get energy. One gram of fats provides nine kilocalories of energy. Fats are stored in the cells of adipose tissue (fatty tissue). This tissue is present beneath the skin and around important organs. It insulates organs against shocks and also maintains body temperature.
Point to remember

Lipids are the organic compound that are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Fats and oils are important types of lipids. "Oil" is liquid at room temperature, while "fat" is solids at room temperature
iii. Fats (Lipids)

Other functions of fats include maintaining healthy skin and hair. Fats help in the digestion, transport of vitamins A, D, E and K in the body. The common sources of fats are butter, ghee, cheese, meat, egg yolk, milk, nuts, etc.

iv. Vitamins

Vitamins are organic food substances found only in living things. With a few exceptions, the body cannot manufacture vitamins. They must be supplied by the diet or in dietary supplements. Vitamins are essential to the normal functioning of our bodies. Vitamins may be divided into two groups: the fat-soluble vitamins (vitamins A, D, E, and K) and the water-soluble vitamins (vitamins B and in C).
iv. Vitamins
Our bodies can store fat-soluble vitamins and can use them when needed. Water-soluble vitamins are not stored in our body.
a. Vitamin A

Vitamin A is also known as retinol, a name given in reference to its participation in the functions of the retina of the eye. This vitamin also participates in the functions of the immune system and helps in growth and reproduction.
a. Vitamin A
Dietary deficiency of vitamin A may cause vision problems and night blindness. Vitamin A deficiency can also affect growth, skin and immune system.
a. Vitamin A
Animal sources of vitamin A are chicken liver, cod liver oil, eggs, butter, milk etc.
a. Vitamin A
Plant sources of vitamin A are sweet potatoes, carrots, spinach, mangoes, oranges, grapefruit etc.

b. Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid)

Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin. It is needed for the growth and repair of body tissues. It helps the body to make collagen, an important protein in skin, cartilage, tendons, ligaments and blood vessels. Vitamin C is essential for healing wounds and for repairing and maintaining bones and teeth.
b. Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid)

Signs of vitamin C deficiency include drying and splitting of hair, inflammation and bleeding of gums, rough, dry and scaly skin, decreased wound-healing, nosebleeds and a decreased ability to fight infection. A severe form of vitamin C deficiency is known as scury. Sources of vitamin C are tomatoes, strawberries, broccoli, cabbage, guava etc.
Scientific Information

Vitamin C is an antioxidant along with vitamin E. Antioxidants block some of the damage caused by free radicals. The build-up of free radicals over time may be responsible for the aging process and can contribute to the development of unhealthy conditions such as cancer, heart disease and arthritis.
c. Vitamin D

Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin. It aids in the absorption of calcium, helping to form and maintain strong bones. The major function of vitamin D is to maintain normal blood levels of calcium and phosphorus. It is also made by the skin. When ultraviolet rays from sunlight strike the skin, they trigger vitamin D synthesis.
c. Vitamin D

Due to deficiency of vitamin D, bones can become thin, brittle and soft. In children, vitamin-D deficiency leads to rickets (a condition in which bones weaken and bow under pressure). In adults, vitamin-D deficiency causes osteomalacia mean "soft bones" thus increasing the risk for fractures in bones. Main sources of vitamin D are cod liver oil, egg yolk, fortified bread cheese etc.

v. Minerals

Minerals are inorganic elements that originate in the Earth and cannot be made in the body. They play important roles in various body functions. Most of the minerals in the human diet come directly from plants, animals and water. The minerals required in the amount of 100mg (milligrams) or more per day are called major minerals e.g. sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus and sulfur.
v. Minerals
The minerals required in amounts less than 100 mg per day are called trace minerals e.g. iron, zinc, copper, chromium, fluoride, iodine, selenium, manganese and molybdenum.
a. Role of Calcium

Calcium is one of the most important and most abundant minerals in the human body. It plays an important role in the development and maintenance of the bones. Calcium is also needed for tooth formation. It plays an important role in blood clotting, transmission of nerve impulses, muscle contraction, and other metabolic activities.
Point to remember
About 99% of the body's calcium is stored in bone tissue. The remaining 1% of the body's calcium circulates in the blood and other body fluids.
a. Role of Calcium
Dairy products are the major source of calcium. Eggs, green leafy vegetables, broccoli, legumes, nuts and whole grains provide calcium but in smaller amounts than dairy products.
Scientific Information
Brittle nails, dry skin and consistent muscle cramping are big signs of calcium deficiency in diet. If there is a calcium deficiency, there is more risk for developing osteoporosis or rickets.
b. Role of Iron

Iron is an important mineral. It is a part of haemoglobin molecule, which helps the red blood cells to transport oxygen to the cells of the body. Iron also helps the immune and central nervous systems. The main sources of iron are red meat, fish, beans, dried fruit, green vegetables and apple.
Point to remember

Low iron levels can cause people to develop anemia i.e. a decrease in the amount of red blood cells or haemoglobin in the blood. In such condition, the blood's ability to carry oxygen is lowered and the patient feels weakness and tiredness.

vi. Dietary Fibers

Dietary fiber is also known as "roughage" or "bulk". It is the part of the human food that is indigestible. It mainly consists of cellulose and is found in vegetables, fruits and cereals. Dietary fiber moves unaltered through the digestive system. There are two types of dietary fiber: insoluble and soluble. Insoluble fiber does not dissolve in water and travels through the small intestine quickly.
vi. Dietary Fibers

Wheat bran, whole grain breads and cereals, as well as the skins of many fruits and vegetables, contain insoluble fiber. Soluble fiber breaks down as it passes through the digestive tract, forming a gel that traps harmful substances e.g. cholesterol. Oats, beans, barley and many fruits and vegetables contain soluble fiber. Dietary fiber speeds up the passage of food through the gut.
vi. Dietary Fibers
So it reduces the risk of constipation and colon cancer. It also absorbs cholesterol and so controls the blood cholesterol level.
vii. Water
Water is the most abundant substance in the human body. We have about 70% water in our body. Water performs many functions. Some are following:
Scientific Information

An average adult requires about two litres water per day. Usually, the water lost through skin, lungs and kidneys is easily replaced by drinking water or eating moist foods. If excess water is lost and not replenished, the condition is called dehydration. In this condition, water moves from extracellular spaces to the blood. Water in cells moves to the extracellular spaces and the cytoplasm becomes more concentrated.
Scientific Information
In severe dehydration, cells cannot function.

a. In our bodies, metabolic reactions can only occur when the reactants are dissolved. Water act as the solvent for reactants of metabolism.

8.4 Balanced Diet

The amount of each component of balanced diet is determined according to the energy requirements. The energy requirements are not same for all. Diet and energy requirements are always related to age, gender and activity of individual.
(i) Relationship of Energy Requirements with Age

During growth period, new cells are formed at a greater rate and cells expend more energy. So the body needs foods that contain more energy. Children at the age of 13-15 years need more food per kilogram of body weight than adults. Similarly, children need more calcium and iron for their growing bones and red blood cells respectively.
(ii) Relationship of Energy Requirements with Gender
Women have a comparatively lower metabolic rate than men of the same age and weight. So men need foods that provide more energy.
(iii) Relationship of Energy Requirements with Activity
People have different lifestyles and varied nature of work. A man with sedentary habits does not require as much energy as the man who remains physically active for most of the day.

8.5 Malnutrition

Taking a diet in which the required nutrients are not in enough quantity or over the required quantity is called malnutrition. Under nutrition is a consequence of consuming low amount of essential nutrients while over nutrition means taking too much nutrients. Severe malnutrition may result in death, heart diseases, constipation and obesity.
8.5 Malnutrition
The major types of malnutrition are Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM), Mineral Deficiency Diseases (MDD) and Over Intake of Nutrients (OIN).
A- Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM)

The term Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM) applies to a condition in which the body is not getting required amounts of proteins or any energy producing nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids). It may also occur when the body cannot absorb such nutrients due to other diseases (e.g. AIDS or cancer). Two important diseases associated with PEM are marasmus and kwashiorkor.
Scientific Information
Soya beans are used as a major source of protein in many different forms and soya milk has been found to be a good substitute for more costly cow or goat milk.
i. Marasmus

This type of PEM occurs in children due to very low intake of carbohydrates, fats and protein. Children suffering from marasmus have very thin bodies. Their body weight is less than 60 percent of the expected weight for their age. They have almost no fats and muscle strength in their bodies. They also suffer from low body temperature and anaemia. Marasmus can be treated by adding all nutrients to the diet.
i. Marasmus
In severe cases, this disease may lead to death.

They also suffer from thinning of hair and loss of teeth. Their body fails to produce antibodies against diseases. Kwashiorkor can be treated by adding proteins to the diet. In severe cases, this disease may also lead to death.

8.6 Human Digestive System

The food we eat consists mostly of large and complex molecules (starch, proteins and lipids). These molecules cannot cross the cell membrane. So, cells cannot use them for energy or growth. Therefore, the food molecules must be broken down to smaller molecules that can pass through cell membrane.
8.6 Human Digestive System

Intake of food or ingestion is followed by digestion. Digestion is defined as "the breakdown of larger, complex and non-diffusible food molecules into smaller, simpler and diffusible molecules by the action of enzymes".
8.6 Human Digestive System

Once the food is digested, it is absorbed. The uptake of diffusible food from the digestive tract into the blood is called absorption. The blood transports the absorbed food to the body tissues, where it diffuses into the cells. Cells utilize the food molecules according to their specialities and needs. Food molecules can be oxidized to get energy or changed to make new materials for growth.
8.6 Human Digestive System

This process is known as assimilation. Not all the food we eat is digested. A considerable amount of food is not digested and it ends in a waste material which the body must get rid of. This elimination or removal of undigested food (faeces) from the body is called egestion.
Scientific Information
Other names for the alimentary canal include the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, digestive tract, alimentary tract and nourishment canal.
8.6 Human Digestive System
Human digestive system consists of a long tube called alimentary canal and associated glands.
