Tongue contains taste buds which can help us to sense the taste of food. Tongue also helps during grinding of food by keeping it between the teeth. It also helps in swallowing process.
Scientific Information

In general terms, the secretion of saliva is called watering of mouth. It is a reflex mechanism controlled by nervous system. Even the sight, smell or hearing of delicious food, stimulate the nervous system which orders for the secretion of saliva.
a. Oral Cavity (Buccal Cavity)

There are three pairs of salivary glands in the oral cavity. These glands secrete saliva. Saliva is a mixture of water, mucous, salts and a digestive enzyme. Mucous lubricates the food. The salt sodium bicarbonate present in saliva, kills the germs and bacteria and makes the food alkaline. The enzyme called salivary amylase begins the chemical digestion of starch and glycogen.
a. Oral Cavity (Buccal Cavity)
It breaks the starch and glycogen into maltose. After the mechanical and partial chemical digestion, the food turns into the form of a ball called bolus.
b. Pharynx and Swallowing

The oral cavity opens into the pharynx. Pharynx is present at the back of oral cavity. Food in the form of bolus is pushed back by the action of tongue. The downward movement of the food from the buccal cavity is called swallowing. The beginning of the swallowing is voluntary but once the food reaches the back of the oral cavity, swallowing becomes automatic or reflex action.
b. Pharynx and Swallowing
The food is forced into and down the oesophagus by peristalsis.
Scientific Information

Pharynx is a passage for both air and food. It provides passages to food from oral cavity to oesophagus. It also provides passages to air from nasal cavity to trachea (windpipe), through an opening called glottis. During swallowing, the top of trachea moves upwards. Due to this action, a flap called epiglottis closes the glottis so that food particles cannot enter the windpipe.
c. Oesophagus

Oesophagus or food pipe is a muscular tube extending from the pharynx to the stomach. It is about 10 inches long. It runs through the neck and thorax between the trachea and vertebral column. Food is passed rapidly through the oesophagus by peristalsis.
c. Oesophagus
Peristalsis: Peristalsis is a wave like contractions and relaxations in the muscular walls of the alimentary canal by which the food is moved along the alimentary canal.
Scientific Information
Sometimes, due to irritation in the oesophagus or stomach, the process of peristalsis is reversed and vomiting occurs. This reversal of peristalsis is called antiperistalsis.
c. Oesophagus
Figure 8.10: Peristalsis in oesophagus
Scientific Information
During swallowing, the soft palate and the uvula move superiorly to close off the nasopharynx, preventing food from entering the nasal cavity.
c. Oesophagus

d. Stomach

Stomach is a sac-like organ and is located between the esophagus and the intestines. It is a muscular, elastic, pear-shaped bag, lying crosswise in the abdominal cavity beneath the diaphragm. It is about 12 inches long and 6 inches wide at its widest point. The stomach's capacity is about one liter.
Scientific Information
Heart burn is the sensation when stomach juices (gastric juice) seep through the cardiac sphincter into the oesophagus.
d. Stomach

Food enters the stomach from the oesophagus. At the junction of the oesophagus and the stomach, there are muscles called cardiac sphincter. The cardiac sphincter prevents food from passing back to the oesophagus.
d. Stomach

The walls of the stomach are thick and muscular. Once the food enters the stomach, its walls contract to churn (break down) the food into smaller particles. This is the mechanical digestion of food. The churning action also produces heat which helps to melt the lipids in the food.
d. Stomach

The inner walls of the stomach have many gastric glands. They secrete gastric juice into the stomach. The gastric juice contains mucus, pepsinogen enzyme and hydrochloric acid. Hydrochloric acid converts the inactive pepsinogen into an active enzyme called pepsin. Pepsin breaks large protein molecules into shorter chains of amino acids called peptides. Hydrochloric acid also kills bacteria present in food.
d. Stomach
After these actions on food, it is converted into a thick soup-like fluid called chyme.
d. Stomach
Figure 8.11: Structure of the Stomach
d. Stomach

The mucus present in gastric juice forms a coating on the inner walls of stomach. It protects the inner lining of stomach from HCl and enzymatic action of pepsin. In this way, the walls are protected from breakdown. The other end of the stomach called the pyloric end empties into first section of the small intestine called duodenum. The pyloric sphincter separates the stomach from the duodenum.
Scientific Information

A hormone called gastrin, controls the secretion of gastric juice. Protein molecules stimulate the endocrine cells of the stomach to secrete gastrin. Blood carries gastrin to the gastric glands to secrete large amount of gastric juice in the stomach.
Scientific Information
Food usually remains in the stomach for three to four hours. Each time the pyloric sphincter opens, about 5 to 15 ml of chyme moves into the small intestine.
e. Small Intestine

Stomach opens into small intestine. Small intestine is an elongated narrow and coiled tube. It is the longest and most important part of human digestive system. It is divided into three parts: (i) Duodenum (ii) Jejunum (iii) Ileum
(i) Duodenum

It is the first part of small intestine, about 12 inches long and curved like 'C'. It receives chyme from the stomach. In duodenum, the chyme meets the bile from the liver and pancreatic juice from the pancreas. Both are alkaline secretions.
(i) Duodenum

Liver as digestive gland: Liver is a large reddish brown gland. It consists of two main lobes, each is further divided into smaller lobes. The liver produces bile which is stored in gall bladdar and secreted into the duodenum through the common bile duct. Bile is a green alkaline liquid without any enzyme. The bile contains water, sodium bicarbonate, excess of calcium and the breakdown products of haemoglobin.
(i) Duodenum
It breaks larger fats into smaller droplets. This process is called emulsification of fats. Bile also neutralizes the acidity of the chyme.
(i) Duodenum

Pancreas as digestive gland: Pancreas is a yellowish organ present beneath the stomach. It is connected to the duodenum. It secretes pancreatic juice into pancreatic duct, which joins the common bile duct before entering the duodenum. Pancreatic juice contains sodium bicarbonate and enzymes. Sodium bicarbonate neutralizes the acidity of chyme.
(i) Duodenum

The enzymes present in pancreatic juice are trypsinogen (inactive enzyme), pancreatic amylase and lipase. The inactive trypsinogen is converted into active trypsin by the duodenal enzyme. Trypsin acts on proteins, which have escaped the action of pepsin and converts them into amino acids. The pancreatic amylase acts on the starch, which have escaped the action of salivary amylase and converts them into simple sugars.
(i) Duodenum
Lipase acts on emulsified fats and converts them into fatty acids and glycerol.
(i) Duodenum
Figure 8.12: Digestive Glands
(ii) Jejunum
Jejunum comes after duodenum and is about 2.4 meters long.
(iii) Ileum

The ileum is about 2.6 meters long. The glands of the ileum secretes intestinal juice. It contains enzymes which break down the leftover undigested proteins, carbohydrates and fats. In this way, the digestion of food is completed in the small intestine.
Absorption of Food

After the complete digestion of food, the end products i.e. amino acids, simple sugars, glycerol and fatty acids are absorbed from the small intestine into the circulatory system. The structure of small intestine is in accordance with its absorptive function. The inner lining of small intestine has large folds. These folds have millions of finger-like projections called villi (Singular: villus).
Absorption of Food
The outer epithelium of villus is made of a single layer of cells. The epithelium of villi also contains microscopic projections called micro villi.
Absorption of Food
The microvilli greatly increase the surface area of the villus. Inside villus, there are blood capillaries and a small lymphatic vessel called lacteal.
Absorption of Food

During absorption, the simple sugars, amino acids, vitamins, minerals and water enter the blood capillaries in the villi. These capillaries open in the hepatic portal vein, which carries the nutrients to the liver. Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the lacteals which pour them into the blood stream.
Absorption of Food
Figure 8.13: Structure of villus
f. Large Intestine
Large intestine is the part of the digestive system where undigested food is collected and converted into faeces. The large intestine is about 1.5 m long and consists of the caecum, colon and rectum.
Scientific Information

The appendix is a small projection emerging from the caecum. In human beings, the appendix has no known function. In some people, the appendix becomes infected. This condition is called 'appendicitis'. For its treatment, the appendix needs to be removed.
f. Large Intestine

(i) Caecum: It is the first part of the large intestine. It receives the mixture from the small intestine and moves it towards the colon. The mixture in caecum contains undigested food, water, some vitamins and some salts.
f. Large Intestine
Figure 8.14: Large Intestine
f. Large Intestine

(ii) Colon: The colon is the longest part of large intestine. The colon has four sections i.e. ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon. As the material travels through the colon, the lining of the colon absorbs most of the water and some vitamins and minerals. The mixture of undigested material, water, dead cells of alimentary canal, bile pigments etc., mixes with mucus and takes the form of faeces.
f. Large Intestine
Through muscular movements of the colon, faeces is pushed into the rectum.
f. Large Intestine
(iii) Rectum: It is the final part of the large intestine. It is where stool is stored before being passed out from anus. It is called egestion.
Scientific Information

Bacteria are present in colon. They break down some of the fibre to produce nutrients for their own survival. They also nourish the cells of the colon. Some vitamins are also produced by them. Thus, the fibre in your diet is extremely important to maintain the long-term health of the colon.
Other Roles of the Liver
The liver produces bile which emulsifies fats and break them into droplets. Besides its digestive function, liver also performs many other functions in the body. For example;
Other Roles of the Liver
(i) It stores glucose as glycogen and provides glucose when required.
Other Roles of the Liver
(ii) It also stores fat-soluble vitamins.
Other Roles of the Liver

(iii) Liver converts amino acids to other organic compounds. In this process, ammonia is produced. Liver converts this harmful compound to less toxic urea, which is then excreted from the body through urine.
Other Roles of the Liver
(iv) It makes many of the body proteins.
Other Roles of the Liver
(v) Toxic substances e.g. alcohol are broken down in liver.
Other Roles of the Liver
(vi) It also breaks the red blood cells which have completed their life spans.
Other Roles of the Liver
(vii) Liver makes vitamin A from carotene.
Other Roles of the Liver
(viii) In cold temperatures, liver carries out basic metabolism at faster rates and so produces heat.

a. Constipation

Constipation is a disorder of the digestive system in which faeces are not eliminated from the body at regular intervals. The symptoms of constipation are passing hard and dry stools, unusual straining at stool and abdominal bloating or discomfort.
a. Constipation
The common causes of constipation include frequent use of spicy food, less intake of vegetables and dietary fibre and insufficient fluid intake.
a. Constipation
Constipation is treated by taking more dietary fibre and water along with diet. Laxative medicines are also used to treat constipation.
Scientific Information
The routine use of laxative medicines is discouraged because patient may become dependent on their use.
b. Diarrhoea

Diarrhoea means that proper amounts of water are not absorbed from colon and the required water leaves the body along with faeces. The main symptoms of diarrhoea are frequent, watery, loose bowel movements, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. Diarrhoea results in dehydration, which means the body lacks enough fluid to function properly.
b. Diarrhoea

Diarrhea is caused by bacterial, viral or parasitic infection of the colon walls. It is treated by consuming adequate amounts of water preferably mixed with salts and nutrients to replace the loss. When diarrhoea is due to bacterial infection, it is treated by administration of antibiotics. Diarrhoea can be prevented by taking sufficient amounts of clean water and food.
c. Ulcers

An ulcer is a small erosion (hole) in the walls of the gut. It usually occurs in the walls of stomach and is called gastric ulcer. It may also develop in duodenum (duodenal ulcer) or oesophagus (oesophageal ulcer). The symptoms of ulcer include abdominal burning and pain, loss of appetite and weight loss.
c. Ulcers
Figure 8.15: Gastric ulcer
c. Ulcers

The basic cause of ulcers is the destruction of the gut wall by hydrochloric acid. Cigarette smoking is also an important cause of ulcer formation. Ulcer is treated with alkaline medicines. Its preventions include avoiding spicy and acidic foods.

9.1 Transport in Plants

Living organisms always require certain materials for their metabolic processes. In a particular environment different types of materials either move in or out of the body of an organism. This movement of molecules into and out of the body or cells of an organism is called transport.
Point to remember

In multi-cellular organisms, an organ system is responsible for the transport of materials. In unicellular organisms there is no such system, however processes, such as, diffusion, osmosis etc. sufficient for the transport of materials.
9.1 Transport in Plants

Unicellular and less complex multicellular organisms do not have any specific organs for transport. They perform this process by simple diffusion or active transport. In more complex animals and plants, there are special organ systems for exchange of material with the environment and for transport of material within the body.
9.1 Transport in Plants

Each and every cell of the body needs food and oxygen and also needs to remove the waste products, it produces during its metabolic activities. However, every cell is not in direct contact with the external sources to get nutrients and remove wastes. Also, the cells are not in direct contact with the organs/ tissues/ cells of the body where these nutrients are formed and wastes are stored.
9.1 Transport in Plants

Hence a system is needed to transport all the needs like O₂, CO₂, nutrients, water etc. and to remove the wastes from the cells. All organisms whether unicellular or multicellular, plants or animals, simple or complex, have a transport system in their bodies. In this unit, we will discuss the process of transport in plants and humans.
9.1 Transport in Plants

Plants transport many substances within the body. Water and dissolved salts are transported from the roots to the shoot through the xylem tissue. The food is transported from the leaves, where it is manufactured, to all other parts of the body through phloem tissue. Similarly, the stored food is transported from storage organs to all other parts.
Absorption of Water and Salts

Water is absorbed by the plants through their roots. Roots are in contact with the soil from where water enters into roots tissues through osmosis. In order to understand the absorption of water and salts by roots, we have to study the internal structure of a root.
Absorption of Water and Salts

The outermost covering of the root i.e. epidermis is a single layer of cells. Many cells of epidermis have tiny hair-like extensions called root hair into the spaces in soil. The root hair are in direct contact with soil water. They provide large surface area to the root for the maximum absorption of water and salts.
Absorption of Water and Salts

The root hair cells have high concentration of salts as compared to their surrounding soil water. They also take in more salts by active transport. Due to this higher concentration of salts in root hair cells, water moves by passive transport i.e. osmosis from soil into the root hair cells. From root hair cells, water goes by osmosis to the other cells of epidermis.
Analysing and Interpreting
Identify root hairs on a growing root of onion, carrot etc.
Absorption of Water and Salts

From epidermis, salts and water move to the cortex of root. It is present just below the epidermis. The innermost boundary of the cortex is the endodermis. The water and salts move to a narrow layer of cells called pericycle. After crossing pericycle, water and salts reach in the innermost region where vascular tissue i.e. xylem and phloem are present. Water and salts enter the xylem of root.
Absorption of Water and Salts
The xylem and phloem of root are connected to the xylem and phloem of the stem.
Absorption of Water and Salts

9.2 Transpiration

Loss of water in the form of vapours from the aerial parts of the plant, is called transpiration. Transpiration occurs mainly through the special openings present in leaf epidermis. These openings are called stomata (Singular: stoma). In leaves, water is present in the xylem tissues. This water moves to the cell walls of mesophyll cells.
9.2 Transpiration
From the moist walls of mesophyll cells, water evaporates into the air spaces of the leaf. These water vapours then move towards the stomata and pass into the outside air.
Point to remember
Some transpiration also occurs through the cuticle present on leaf epidermis and through special openings called lenticels present in the stems of some plants.
Scientific Information
More than 90% water absorbed by the roots is ultimately lost to the atmosphere through transpiration.
9.2 Transpiration
Figure 9.2: Events of Transpiration
9.2.1 Stomatal Control of Transpiration

Transpiration occurs through stomata which allows the water vapours to transpire into the environment. When there is sufficient water, stomata remain open allowing transpiration to take place. Each stoma is lined by two bean shaped cells called guard cells. Guard cells are the only epidermal cells which contain chloroplasts. Stomata open and close when the turgor pressure of guard cells changes.
9.2.1 Stomatal Control of Transpiration
Stoma opens when guard cells are turgid, while it closes when guard cells become flaccid.
Scientific Information
Desert plants have very few or no stomata. Their leaves are modified into thorns to minimize transpiration.
Point to remember
During daytime, movement of potassium ions in guard cells also increases their solute concentration.
9.2.1 Stomatal Control of Transpiration

During day time, guard cells do photosynthesis and prepare glucose. So the solute concentration remains high in guard cells. Therefore water moves in them and they become turgid. In turgid state, the inner walls of guard cells move outward and stoma opens. At evening, the glucose concentration in guard cells falls. Due to this, water also moves from guard cells and they lose turgor (state of turgidity).
9.2.1 Stomatal Control of Transpiration
Their inner sides touch each other and the stoma closes.
9.2.1 Stomatal Control of Transpiration
Figure 9.3: Opening and closing of stoma
9.2.2 Factors Affecting Rate of Transpiration
The rate of transpiration depends on many factors. Some of the important factors and their effects are as follows:
9.2.2 Factors Affecting Rate of Transpiration

i. Light: Light directly controls the opening and closing of stomata. In strong light, stomata are open and the rate of transpiration become high. In low light and darkness, stomata get closed and transpiration stops.
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration
ii. Temperature: With a rise in temperature, water evaporates more rapidly. So transpiration rate increases. At lower temperature, the rate of transpiration is low.
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration

iii. Humidity: Presence of water vapours in air is called humidity. In low humidity, there are less water vapours in the atmosphere. So the rate of the loss of water vapours from leaf is high. When there is higher humidity in atmosphere, the rate of transpiration becomes low.
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration
iv. Soil Moisture: If more water is present in the soil, more absorption will take place through the roots and rate of transpiration will increase.
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration

v. Wind: Air in motion is called wind. If the air is not moving, the water molecules transpiring out of stomata remain in the surrounding air which becomes humid. It stops further water molecule to come out and the rate of transpiration is reduced. If air is moving, the transpired water is rapidly removed from the leaf surroundings and there is space for more water vapours to come out of stomata.
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration
This increases the rate of transpiration.
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration

vi. Number and Distribution of Stomata: Leaves with more surface area have more stomata than the leaves with narrow blades. The greater the number of stomata on a leaf, the higher would be the transpiration rate. In most land plants, the number of stomata is greater on the lower leaf surface than on the upper surface. Therefore, more transpiration occurs from the lower surface
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration

Transpiration is a vital process in the life of plants. It prevents the leaves from overheating and keeps them cool. Roots constantly absorb water. Transpiration helps the plant to get rid of excess water and salts. Transpiration from leaves creates a pulling force on the water in xylem tissues of stem and root. This pulling force causes the water to rise up in the xylem tissues.
Science, Technology and Society

The plant living in areas with adequate water content in the soil (due to irrigation or rainfall) have better nutrients uptake from the soil. They also have efficient transport of nutrients within the plant body. Write a short summary to explain the role of water in soil with respect to the distribution of nutrients in the plant.
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration
Due to transpiration, the mesophyll cells always remain moist. This helps in gaseous exchange especially the absorption of CO₂ which is essential for photosynthesis.
9.2.3 Significance of Transpiration

Although transpiration plays an important role in the normal functioning of the plants, it may prove harmful when there is deficiency of water in the soil. In such conditions, transpiration may result in wilting. Transpiration is important for plants but excessive loss of water is harmful. Therefore, transpiration is considered as a necessary evil.
Scientific Information

One of the terminology related to transpiration is "Evapotranspiration". It is defined as loss of water from the soil both by evaporation from the soil surface and by transpiration from the leaves of the plants growing on it. Factors that affect the rate of evapotranspiration include the amount of solar radiation, atmospheric vapor pressure, temperature, wind and soil moisture.
9.3 Transportation of Water

Transpiration of water from the leaves creates a pulling force in the leaves. This pulling force is called transpirational pull. The transpirational pull occurs when mesophyll cells of leaves lose water vapours, more water enters in them from the xylem vessels of the leaf. The xylem vessels and leaf are linked with the xylem vessels of stem and root. There is an unbroken column of water in xylem vessels.
9.3 Transportation of Water

This unbroken water column is mainly due to three reasons; (i) the attractive forces among water molecules, (ii) narrow diameter of xylem vessels and (iii) the force by which water molecules are adhered to the walls of xylem vessels.
9.3 Transportation of Water
Figure 9.4: Transport of water in plants
9.3 Transportation of Water

When one water molecule moves up in the xylem of the leaf, it produces a tension on the entire water column in the xylem of leaf, stem and root. As a result, the entire water column is pulled upwards.

9.4 Translocation of Food in Plants

We know that phloem tissue is responsible for the translocation (transport) of food among different parts of the plant body. The translocation of food in plants was explained by Ernst Munch (a Germen biologist) in 1930. He called his explanation as the theory of Pressure Flow. According to this theory, the dissolved food flows from a source to a sink. The sources include photosynthetic tissues (e.g.
9.4 Translocation of Food in Plants

mesophyll of leaves) and storage tissues (e.g. roots). Sinks include the sites of food utilization (e.g. growing tips of roots and stems) and the storage tissues. The following are the steps of translocation of food in plants.
Point to remember
The liquid in the phloem consist of 10-25% dry matter of which 90% of sucrose and about 1% is nitrogenous compounds.
9.4 Translocation of Food in Plants
i. At the source site, food (sucrose) enters the sieve tubes of phloem by active transport. Companion cells of phloem provide ATP energy for this transport.
9.4 Translocation of Food in Plants
ii. Due to higher solute concentration in sieve tubes than the nearby xylem tissue, water flows into sieve tubes by osmosis.
9.4 Translocation of Food in Plants
Figure 9.5: The translocation of Food in Plants
9.4 Translocation of Food in Plants
iii. Due to the movement of water, the turgor pressure of sieve tubes increases and the solution of food flows towards the sink
9.4 Translocation of Food in Plants
iv. At the sink, food is actively removed from sieve tubes. Water also moves from the sieve tubes by osmosis.
9.4 Translocation of Food in Plants
In this way, the turgor pressure in sieve tubes falls down, causing a flow of mass from the higher pressure at the source to the lower pressure at the sink.

9.5 Transport in Human Beings

Like other organisms, human beings need a transport system to deliver oxygen, nutrients and other substances to all cells in the body and to take away waste products from them. The transport system consists of the blood (the transporting fluid), the heart (the pumping organ) and the blood vessels.
Point to remember
In humans and other animals, the lymphatic system also works for the transport of materials. It consists of special vessels called lymphatic vessels, which work in association with blood vessels.
9.5.1 Blood

In human beings and many other animals, blood is a red fluid which circulates through blood vessels (arteries, veins and capillaries) and heart. Blood is a type of connective tissue and is composed of two parts i.e. plasma and cells or cell-like bodies.
Activities
Observe and investigate transpiration in potted plant under a bell jar/ polythene bag. Investigate, using a suitable stain, the pathway of water in a cut stem.
a. Plasma

If blood is taken in a test tube and allowed to stand for a few minutes, a yellow coloured liquid is separated from the cells and cell-like bodies. Cellular components settle down and pale yellow liquid remains at the top. This yellow coloured material is called plasma. It constitutes about 55% by volume of blood. It contains about 90% water and 10% dissolved substances.
a. Plasma
Out of these substances, about 7% are different types of proteins generally called plasma proteins.
a. Plasma
Figure 9.6: Composition of Blood
a. Plasma
0.9-1% of plasma is made of different inorganic salts, while 2% consists of food materials, hormones, waste products, etc. Plasma performs various functions:
Scientific Information
pH of human blood is 7.4 and the total weight of blood is about 1/12th of our body weight.
a. Plasma

Plasma keeps all the tissues moist. • Plasma of the blood transports nutrients, water, salts, hormones and waste materials. • Plasma helps in regulating body temperature. • Small amounts of oxygen are also carried by plasma. Most of the CO₂ is carried by plasma. • Plasma proteins e.g. albumins maintain the osmotic pressure of blood. • Important plasma proteins called antibodies defend the body against pathogens.
a. Plasma
• Another plasma protein fibrinogen is responsible for blood clotting.
Scientific Information
When a blood clots, fibrinogen is separated from blood plasma. The rest of blood is called serum.
b. Blood Cells and cell-like bodies
Blood contains cells i.e. red blood cells and white blood cells and also contains cell-like bodies i.e. blood platelets. Both make about 45% of blood by volume.
Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes)

RBCs are the most numerous of all the blood cells. It gives the red colour to the blood due to the presence of red pigment, haemoglobin. A cubic millimetre of blood contains about 5 million RBCs. In humans, a mature RBC is biconcave, rounded cell and contains no nucleus.

Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes)

Before and immediately after birth, RBCs are formed in liver and spleen. In adults, they are formed in the red bone marrow of short bones (sternum, ribs and vertebrae). The average life span of a red blood cell is about 120 days, after which they are removed from the blood by the spleen and liver.
Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes)
RBCs are red because they contain a red protein, haemoglobin. Haemoglobin carries oxygen and little amounts of CO₂ in the blood.
Scientific Information

RBCs are specialized cells. 95% of their cytoplasm is composed of haemoglobin. Remaining 5% contains ezymes, other proteins and salts. It has been estimated that a single RBC contains about 2 billion molecules of haemoglobin.
White Blood Cells (Leucocytes)

White blood cells are colourless as they do not contain any pigment. They are irregular in shape and are nucleated. Each cubic millimetre of blood contains about 7000 to 8000 WBCs. Their life span is very short i.e. from 7 hours to a maximum of 3 days (with the exception of some lymphocytes which stay for longer periods).
Scientific Information
The increased number of WBCs in the blood shows the level of infection in the body.
Scientific Information
WBCs die in the process of killing the germs. The dead cells accumulate and make the white substance called pus, seen at infection sites.
White Blood Cells (Leucocytes)

There are five different types of WBCs. They are the part of immune system and defend our body against diseases. They circulate and are transported to an area where infection has developed. Some WBCs kill pathogens (bacteria, virus etc) by engulfing them. Some of them also produce inflammation at the site of infection. While some of the WBCs make antibodies against pathogens.
Scientific Information

We ingest thousands of germs daily especially through our mouth and nose but still we remain healthy. Thanks to WBCs which engulf these disease carrying agents and destroy them. In this effort they themselves are also destroyed. Disease starts when the immune system is weak and germs are stronger and more in number.
Platelets (Thrombocytes)

Platelets are not true cells. They are fragments of cytoplasm pinched off from certain bone marrow cells. Each cubic millimetre of blood contains about 150,000 to 450,000 platelets. Their life span is about 7-12 days.
Platelets (Thrombocytes)

Platelets help in blood clotting. When the blood vessls are damaged, the blood start oozing out, they gather at the site. They release a substance which converts plasma protein fibrinogen into threads of insoluble fibrin. These threads make a mesh in which platelets and other blood cells are entangled to make a clot and stop the blood flow from the wound.

9.5.2 Blood Disorders
In human beings, many disorders are associated with blood. Here we will discuss only two of them.
(i) Leukaemia

Leukaemia or blood cancer is a disease in which leucocytes or WBCs increase abnormally. Their number rises to several hundred thousand per cubic millimetre of blood. These WBCs start engulfing and destroying the normal cells including the RBCs and platelets. This is why a person suffering from leukaemia suffers from severe anaemia.
(i) Leukaemia
Leukemic cells also attack bones causing severe pain and make them weak and fragile due to which they are easily fractured.
(i) Leukaemia
Leukaemia can be cured by the transplant of bone marrow which is very expensive. To save the life of a person, frequent blood transfusions are required.
(ii) Thalassaemia

It is a genetically transmitted disease from parents to children. A person suffering from this disease has a defective mechanism of producing haemoglobin. The defective haemoglobin cannot transport oxygen. This causes severe anaemia and the patient becomes very weak. Spleen enlargement is also observed. The blood of these patients needs to be replaced regularly with the normal blood of donors.
(ii) Thalassaemia
Bone marrow transplant is not very effective in this disorder.
Scientific Information
Thalassaemia is made of two Greek words; "Thalassa" means sea and "Haem" means blood. It is named so because this disorder was originally found in people living on the shores of Mediterranean Sea.
9.5.3 Blood Group Systems

Blood group is determined by the type of antigen present on the surface of the RBCs. An antigen is a substance that stimulates the production of antibodies. Antigens that are normally present in the body provoke no response. However, when foreign antigens enter the body, the WBCs respond by producing antibodies against them.
a. ABO Blood Group System
ABO blood group system was discovered in 1900 by Karl Land Steiner. A human being may have any one of the following blood groups:
a. ABO Blood Group System

These blood groups are due to the presence of certain specific antigens on the surface of RBCs. A person having antigen A has blood group A, a person having antigen B has blood group B, a person having both the antigens has blood group AB and a person having neither antigen A nor antigen B has blood group O.
a. ABO Blood Group System

On the other hand, a person having blood group A contains anti-B antibodies (antibodies against antigen B) in his blood. Similarly, a person with blood group B contains anti-A antibodies (antibodies against antigen-A). A person with blood group AB does not have any antibodies and a person with blood group O has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

9.5.4 Blood Transfusion in ABO System

Before blood transfusion, it is checked that both the donor and the recipient have the same blood groups. If a person with blood group A receives blood group B, the anti-B antibodies present in recipient's blood will at once recognize the antigen B present on RBCs of donated blood.
Point to remember

Blood transfusion means transferring blood from one person to other. During blood transfusion, infectious diseases (AIDS, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, etc.) can also pass from donor to recipient. That is why, strict screening of donors' blood is done before transfusion.
9.5.4 Blood Transfusion in ABO System
The anti-B antibodies of recipient will react with the B antigens on the donated RBCs and the blood will coagulate. The coagulated blood blocks the flow of blood through blood vessels.
9.5.4 Blood Transfusion in ABO System

The same is true for a person with blood group B transfused with blood group A. Anti-A antibody present in recipient's blood will coagulate with RBCs having antigen-A of donated blood. A person with blood group AB accepts all types of blood. A person with blood group O can only be given the blood group O, because blood group O has anti-A as well as anti-B antibodies.
Rh Blood Group System

This system was discovered by Karl Land Steiner in 1930's. This system is based on the presence or absence of an antigen called Rh factor or Rh antigen (first discovered in Rhesus monkey) on RBCs. Those having it are Rh+ve and those lacking it are Rh-ve.
Blood Transfusion in Rh System

Rh+ve blood group can be transfused to Rh+ve recipient because both have Rh antigen. Similarly Rh-ve blood group can be given to Rh-ve donors. If an Rh-ve person receives Rh+ve blood, he will get Rh antigens. His blood will produce anti-Rh antibodies against Rh antigens and it will result in coagulation. But an Rh+ve person can receive Rh-ve blood.

9.6 Human Heart

Human heart (Greek "Cardium") is a conical, muscular pumping organ. It is present in the chest cavity, behind the breast bone (sternum) between the two lungs. It is felt on the left side because the left chamber of the heart i.e. (left ventricle) is the largest chamber.
Structure of the Heart

Heart is covered by a tough double membrane called pericardium. It protects the heart from over extension. Both membranes of pericardium are separated by a small cavity filled with pericardial fluid. This fluid lubricates the heart during movement.
Structure of the Heart

The heart of birds and mammals has two sides i.e. left and right sides which are divided by a septum (wall). Each side of the heart is divided into an upper and lower chamber. Each upper chamber is called atrium and each lower chamber is called ventricle. So, there are two atria i.e. left and right atria and there are two ventricles i.e. left and right ventricles.
Structure of the Heart
The atria are thin-walled while the ventricles are thick-walled.
Structure of the Heart

Right atrium communicates with right ventricle through a valve called tricuspid valve (having three flaps of muscles) and left atrium opens into left ventricle through a bicuspid valve (having two flaps). Bicuspid valve is also known as mitral valve. These valves control the blood flow and prevent blood from flowing back to atria. A semilunar valve is present between each ventricles and large vessels.
Structure of the Heart
Semilunar valves prevent blood from flowing back into the ventricles.
Circulation of Blood in Heart Chambers

The right side of the heart receives deoxygenated blood from body and sends it to the lungs while the left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and sends it to the body. It means that human heart works as a double pump.
Circulation of Blood in Heart Chambers

The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the whole body through venae cavae (largest veins). This blood is pumped to right ventricle through tricuspid valve. When right ventricle contracts, the deoxygenated blood is pumped to the lungs through pulmonary arteries.
Scientific Information
In birds and mammals, the oxygenated and deoxygenated blood is completely separated. Deoxygenated blood remains on the right side and oxygenated on left side of the heart.
Circulation of Blood in Heart Chambers

The oxygenated blood from lungs comes back to the left atrium through pulmonary veins. From here, this oxygenated blood is pumped to left ventricle via bicuspid valve. When the left ventricle contracts, the oxygenated blood is pumped into aorta (the largest artery) which distributes it to the whole body through a network of arteries.
Circulation of Blood in Heart Chambers

Circulation of Blood in Heart Chambers

The flow of blood from heart to lungs and then from lungs to heart is called pulmonary circulation. Similarly, the flow of blood from heart to the body tissues and then from body tissues to heart is called systemic circulation. The blood in pulmonary circulation is at lower pressure than the blood in the systemic circulation. Due to high pressure in systemic circulation, blood can reach all body parts.
Circulation of Blood in Heart Chambers
On the other hand, due to low pressure in pulmonary circulation, blood flows in lungs in slow speed. It gives sufficient time for gaseous exchange to occur in lungs.
Cardiac Cycle / Heartbeat

One contraction and one relaxation of the heart is called a cardiac cycle. It makes one heartbeat. Contraction of heart is termed as systole and relaxation as diastole. One complete cycle takes 0.8 seconds. Normal rate of heartbeat in a healthy human being is 72 times per minute. This is also called the heart rate.
Cardiac Cycle / Heartbeat

(i) The first phase is called systole. It occurs when both ventricles contract to pump the blood into pulmonary arteries and aorta. Due to this contraction, tricuspid and bicuspid valves close and semilunar valves open. During systole "lubb" sound is produced due to the closing of tricuspid and bicuspid valves.
Cardiac Cycle / Heartbeat

(ii) The second phase is called diastole. It occurs immediately after systole when both atria relax so that blood enters the atria. Due to this, tricuspid and bicuspid valves open and semilunar valves close. Contraction of the atria fills the ventricles. During diastole "dubb" sound is produced due to the closing semilunar valves.
Cardiac Cycle / Heartbeat

Pulse

Heart rate can be measured by feeling the pulse. A pulse is a series of expansion waves in an artery caused by the contractions of the left ventricle. When the ventricle contracts blood rushes through the arteries. The elastic walls of arteries expand. The arteries in wrists are close to the surface. Therefore, pulse can be felt easily here. Pulse rate is an easy way to understand the condition of heart.

Blood Vessels

We have studied that blood moves from the heart to the whole body and from the whole body to the heart. All this circulation takes place through a specialized system of vessels. Arteries, veins and capillaries are the three types of blood vessels.
(i) Arteries

The vessels which carry blood away from the heart towards organs are called arteries. All the arteries carry oxygenated blood except pulmonary arteries which carry deoxygenated blood to lungs. The walls of an artery are made of three layers. Outer elastic layer allows the artery to expand and withstand the pressure of blood. Middle thick layer is made of smooth muscles and elastic fibres.
(i) Arteries
Inner endothelium is comparatively thinner layer. The hollow internal cavity in which the blood flows is called lumen.
Scientific Information
Colour of the arteries appears to be red due to the bright red oxygenated blood flowing through them.
(i) Arteries

Aorta is the largest artery of the body which arises from the left ventricle. Many arteries arise from aorta. Arteries enter organs and divide into smaller branches called arterioles. Arterioles enter tissues and break up into capillaries.
(i) Arteries
Figure 9.11: Blood vessels
(ii) Capillaries

Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels. Their walls are formed of single layer of cells called endothelium. This layer is so thin and permeable that water, nutrients and gases can pass through it to enter the tissue fluid.
(ii) Capillaries
Carbon dioxide and other wastes can diffuse it from tissue fluid into blood. The network of capillaries is so extensive that each of the body cells lies close to a capillary.
(ii) Capillaries
In tissues, capillaries unite to form small veins called venules. The venules unite to form veins.
(iii) Veins

Veins are the vessels which carry blood from organs to the heart. All the veins carry deoxygenated blood except pulmonary veins which carry oxygenated blood from lungs. Walls of the veins are composed of the same three layers but middle layer is thinner. They are less elastic as they do not have to bear pressure.
(iii) Veins

Veins also have valves which allow the flow of blood in one direction i.e. towards heart and prevent backward flow. The largest veins in the body are vena cava. Superior vena cava brings deoxygenated blood from head and upper region of the body and inferior vana cava brings blood from lower parts of the body to the heart.
Scientific Information
A capillary is so thin that RBCs can pass through it in a single row at a time.
General Plan of Human Blood Circulatory System
All the arteries make the arterial system. Similarly, all the veins make the venous system.
Arterial System

As you have already studied that left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into aorta. Aorta gives branches in the form of arteries. The first arteries branching off from the aorta are coronary arteries. These arteries supply the oxygenated blood and food to heart itself.
Arterial System

Aorta then forms an arch which, before descending down, gives off three branches which supply blood to head, shoulders and arms. After it, aorta descends down along with vertebral column. Here, it is called dorsal aorta. It gives off many arteries. For example coeliac artery supplies blood to stomach and spleen, mesenteric arteries to duodenum, pancreas, intestine and rectum.
Arterial System
Similarly, hepatic artery supplies blood to liver and pair of renal arteries to kidneys. The aorta then bifurcates to form right and left iliac arteries which supply blood to right and left legs.
Arterial System
Pulmonary artery originates from right ventricle and carries deoxygenated blood to lungs.
Venus System

The deoxygenated blood is poured into right atrium through two major veins superior vena cava and inferior vena cava. Superior vena cava is formed by the union of many pair of veins from head, shoulders and arms.
Venus System

The inferior vena cava is made of many veins from parts of the lower region. For example, two femoral veins from legs empty into inferior vena cava. Renal veins carry blood from the kidneys. The hepatic portal vein carries blood from alimentary canal to the liver. From liver, a hepatic vein carries blood to the inferior vena cava. From heart walls, deoxygenated blood returns to right atrium through, coronary veins.
Venus System
Pulmonary veins originate from lungs and bring oxygenated blood to left atrium.

Discovery of Blood Circulation

Pioneers of discovering blood circulation are Ibn al Nafees and William Harvey. Many other names are also included in the list but these two gave true, experimentally supported details of the process.
Ibn-Al-Nafees (1210-1288)

Blood circulation in human beings was first described by a Muslim anatomist Ibn-al-Nafees. He studied medicine at Al-Nouri Al-Kabeer Hospital in Damascus. Later, he moved to Cairo where he took up medicine as a career. He was the first to explain the pulmonary blood circulation. He discovered the central role of the heart in the whole circulatory system.
Ibn-Al-Nafees (1210-1288)
Furthermore, Ibn Al-Nafees explained that blood was purified in the lungs.
William Harvey (1578-1657)

Harvey was an English physician who was the first in the Western world to describe correctly the systemic circulation and properties of blood. He demonstrated that heart and blood vessels form a continuous and closed system of circulation.

9.7 Cardiovascular Disorders

The diseases that involve the heart or blood vessels (arteries and veins) are collectively called cardiovascular disorders. These disorders are one of the leading causes of death in the world. Heart and arteries are subjected to many types of damages. Some common disorders are given below.
(i) Atherosclerosis (narrowing of arteries)

It is characterized by the deposition of fatty material e.g. cholesterol inside the arteries. Due to this deposition, the lumen (interior) of the artery becomes narrow and blood flows with difficulty. Later, the artery may completely be blocked. If this blockage is in a coronary artery, it may result in myocardial infarction.
(i) Atherosclerosis (narrowing of arteries)
Some obvious reasons of atherosclerosis are hypertension, smoking, diabetes mellitus and increased lipid level in blood.
(ii) Arteriosclerosis (hardening of arteries)

It is the hardening of the arteries due to the deposition of calcium in the walls of the arteries. Such artery cannot expand when blood is pumped with pressure into it with systole. This inflexibility of the artery makes the heart to work harder. This disorder occurs with increasing age. It generally occurs when atherosclerosis is severe.
(iii) Myocardial Infarction (heart attack)

The term myocardial infarction is derived from myocardium (heart muscle) and infarction (tissue death). Myocardial infarction occurs when coronary artery or its arteriole has some blockage (atherosclerosis) and blood cannot reach heart muscle. So, the part of heart muscles cannot get the required oxygen and die.
(iii) Myocardial Infarction (heart attack)

Chest pain is the most common symptom of myocardial infarction in which patient feels tightness, pressure, or squeezing in chest. The symptom of chest pain due to lack of oxygen supply to the heart muscle is called angina pectoris. Pain radiates most often to the left arm. It may also move to the lower jaw, neck, right arm, and back.
Scientific Information
Sometime heart attack occurs without symptoms of chest pain. It is called silent heart attack. It is more common in the elderly and in patients with diabetes.
(iii) Myocardial Infarction (heart attack)

Myocardial infarction can be prevented by maintaining a healthy weight with a healthy diet, avoiding smoking and exercising regularly. The conditions that lead to myocardial infarction e.g. high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes should be controlled.

Treatment
Immediate treatment of myocardial infarction includes oxygen supply, aspirin, and sublingual tablet of glyceryl trinitrate.
Treatment

For treating myocardial infarction, the blocked artery is opened by a technique called angioplasty. In this treatment a balloon-tip catheter is passed in the artery. At the site of blockage, the balloon is inflated. It clears the blockage and the artery opens. A metallic ring called stent is placed at the site so that artery remains open.
Treatment

Another treatment of myocardial infarction is called bypass surgery. In this treatment a vessel is taken from some other part of the body and is grafted from aorta to the coronary artery. This vessel starts supplying blood to the heart muscles bypassing the original blocked artery.

Introduction
Modern world in which we live is the world of chemicals. We all depend upon different chemicals, which are necessary for our survival.
Introduction
Chemistry is the study of matter and the ways in which different forms of matter combine with each other. Chemistry has a wide applications and serving the humanity and nature.
Introduction

The development of chemistry has provided us a lot of facilities in our life, For example, Petrochemicals, medicines and drugs, papers, plastics, paints, color pigments, soap, detergents etc. The study of chemistry also provides knowledge and techniques to improve our health and environment and to explore and conserve the natural resources.
Introduction
In previous grades, you have learned about the matter, element, compound, mixtures etc. In this unit, you will study different branches of chemistry, basic definitions and concepts of chemistry.
Muslim Period 600 – 1600 AD

The science of chemistry grew and flourished in early civilization of the world. The Egyptians, the Greeks, the Romans and the Muslims contributed much to the science of chemistry. The Muslims made a rich contribution to the knowledge in chemistry. They spread like shining stars on the horizon of the world of science. They made effective and invaluable services in the field of chemistry.
Muslim Period 600 – 1600 AD
This period of Muslims is almost 1000 years long (600 – 1600AD).
Muslim Period 600 – 1600 AD
The principal goals of the Muslim chemists were,
Muslim Period 600 – 1600 AD
1. To find out methods to prolong life. • 2. Looking for ways to change base metals (such as Lead) into Gold. • 3. To find physical evidences to support religious and philosophical beliefs.
Muslim Period 600 – 1600 AD
Though they failed in doing so but they laid the foundation of the laboratory methods. These methods are still used in the modern chemistry.
Muslim Period 600 – 1600 AD

The Muslim scientists discovered many elements e.g. Arsenic (As), Antimony (Sb) and Bismuth (Bi) etc. They developed and used many laboratory instruments e.g. funnels, crucible etc. Many new chemicals processes were also introduced by muslim scientists e.g. filtration, fermentation, distillation etc. Thus, this period provides basis for the modern chemistry.
Muslim Period 600 – 1600 AD

The period of Muslims is generally called the period of “Al - Chemists” in the history of chemistry. Muslim scientists presented chemistry as purely “experimental or practical science”. Some well known Muslim scientists and their achievements are mentioned here:
i) Jabir Ibn Hayyan (721-815 A.D)

Jabir Ibn Hayyan is generally known as the father of the chemistry. He was probably the first scientist who had a well established laboratory. He invented experimental methods such as distillation, sublimation, filtration, extraction of metals etc. He prepared Hydrochloric acid, Nitric acid and white lead.
ii) Muhammad Ibn-e-Zakariya Al-Razi (864-930 A.D)

Al-Razi was a physician, chemist and a philosopher. He wrote 26 books but the most famous book was “Al-Asrar”. In this book, he discussed the different processes of Chemistry. He was the first chemist to divide the chemical compounds into four types and also divides the substances into living and non-living origin. He prepared alcohol by fermentation.
iii) Al - Beruni (973 – 1048 A.D)

He made greater contribution in the field of Physics, Meta-physics, Mathematics, Geography, astronomy and History. In the field of Chemistry, he introduced the different chemical procedures and chemical combinations. He determined the densities of different substances.
iv) Ibne - Sina (980 – 1037 A.D)

Ibne - Sina is generally known as the Aristotle of the Muslim’s world. He is famous for his contributions in the fields of Medicine, Mathematics, Astronomy, Medicinal chemistry and Philosophy. He is the first scientist who rejected the idea, that base metals can be converted into Gold. He wrote more than hundred books. These books were taught in the Europe for centuries.
Definition of Chemistry

Chemistry is a branch of physical science; it includes the study of materials and substances of the world in which we live. Chemistry deals with the composition, structure and properties of matter, the changes occurring in matter and the laws and principles under which these changes occur.
1.1 Branches of Chemistry
The field of chemistry is very vast. To cover all the areas of chemistry, it is divided into different branches.
BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY
Concerned with the relationship between the physical properties of substances along with the chemical changes in them.
BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY
Study of those compounds which contains Carbon and hydrogen called hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY
Deals with the study of all the elements and compounds, except hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY
Deals with the study of qualitative (type / kind) and quantitative (amount / nature) analysis of matter.
BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY
Deals with the study of techniques and chemical processes for the preparation of different industrial products e.g. cement, glass, fertilizers etc.
BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY
Concerned with the study of nucleus, changes occurring in the nucleus, properties of the particles present in the nucleus and the emission or absorption of radiation from the nucleus.
BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY
Concerned with the study of synthesis, composition, decomposition and chemical reaction of substances, which take place in the living organisms.
BRANCHES OF CHEMISTRY
Concerned with the interaction of chemical substances/processes with the environment and their impact on it.

1.2 Basic Definitions: Matter, Substance, Element, Compound and Mixture

All the things present around us, in the universe, are made up of matter. Matter is defined as anything that has mass and occupies space. The quantity of matter in an object is its mass. We can see that almost everything in the universe is made up of matter because they have masses and occupy volumes. A few examples of matter are the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe. Man himself is matter.
1.2 Basic Definitions: Matter, Substance, Element, Compound and Mixture

A piece of matter in pure form is called substance. Pure water is an example of substance, regardless of its sources, have exactly the same composition and properties. All materials may be classified into pure substances (elements, compounds) and impure substances (mixtures).
Society, Technology and Science

In 1924, de Broglie put forward the theory of dual nature of matter i.e. matter has both the properties of particles as well as waves. He explained the background of two ideas. He advocated that these two systems could not remain detached from each other. By mathematical evidences, he proved that every moving object is attached with waves and every wave has particle nature as well.
Society, Technology and Science
It formulated a basis to understand particle nature of matter.
(i) Elements

An Element is a pure substance which cannot be split up into other simpler substances by any ordinary physical or chemical processes. For example, Gold is an element and it can never be converted into any other simpler substance by an ordinary physical or chemical reaction. The fundamental unit of an element is the atom.
(i) Elements
Scientists have discovered approximately 118 elements, out of which 92 are naturally occurring elements, while the rest have been artificially prepared in the laboratory.
(i) Elements

Elements are made up of particles. An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. Each element consists of only one kind of atoms. Atoms of a particular element are same to each other but different from the atoms of other elements.
Symbols of Elements

In 1814, Berzelius suggested the system for representing elements with symbols. The shortest name of an element is called symbol. In most cases, the first letter of the name of an element is taken in capital letter as the symbol. In some cases, where the first letter has already been used, then the initial letters in capital together with a small any other letter from its name are used.

(ii) Compounds Compound is a pure substance consist of two or more different types of elements chemically combined together in a fixed ratio by mass. In the formation of a compound, the component elements must undergo chemical changes. The properties of the compound are different from the elements from which it is formed. For example water (H₂O) is a compound. It is made up of two elements, hydrogen and oxygen.

1.3 Atomic Number, Mass Number, Relative Masses & Chemical Formulae

It has been found that the atoms of one element differ from those of other elements by the number of protons in their nuclei. No two elements have the same number of protons. As the atom is electrically neutral, so they have the same number of electrons, as the number of protons. The number of neutrons in the atoms of an element may be different and cannot be used to characterize the atom.
1.3 Atomic Number, Mass Number, Relative Masses & Chemical Formulae
Elements are therefore arranged in periodic table on the basis of number of protons in their nucleus. This number of protons is called the atomic number. It is represented by the symbol Z.

The atomic number of an element is the number of protons present in the nucleus of one atom of that element.
1.3 Atomic Number, Mass Number, Relative Masses & Chemical Formulae
Hydrogen, carbon and oxygen contain one, six and eight protons in their nucleus respectively. Thus, the atomic number of hydrogen, carbon and oxygen are one, six and eight respectively.

The mass number of an atom is equal to the sum of the number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus.

If we measure the mass of an atom in grams or kilograms, it will be an extremely small value (10⁻²⁴ to 10⁻²² g). Measuring such a small masses are not only impossible but are also impractical to work with. For that purpose, atomic masses are expressed by comparing with a mass of standard atom. The atom chosen nowadays, as the standard for comparison, is that of carbon-12, which has a mass of exactly 12 units.
1.2.3 Relative Atomic Mass and Atomic Mass Unit
The relative atomic mass of an element is the mass of an atom of that element relative to the mass of 1/12th of C-12.

(i) Empirical Formula

The empirical formula of a chemical compound is the simplest formula which shows the smallest whole number ratio of the atoms, of the different elements present in a compound. It may not be the actual formula of the compound. For example, the actual formula of benzene is C₆H₆. Benzene has the simplest ratio of 1:1. So, its empirical formula is CH. The actual formula of glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆.
(i) Empirical Formula
Glucose has the simplest ratio of 1:2:1. So, its empirical formula is CH₂O.

Molecular formula shows the actual numbers of atoms of different elements present in one molecule of that compound. For example, Molecular formula of Glucose = C₆H₁₂O₆. Molecular formula of Benzene = C₆H₆.
(ii) Molecular Formula
Molecular formula is derived from empirical formula by the following relationship. Molecular formula = n (Empirical Formula). Where n = 1, 2, 3, 4.... and so on.
(ii) Molecular Formula
For example the molecular formula of benzene is, Molecular formula = n (Empirical Formula). Where the value of ‘n’ in this case is 6, Molecular formula = 6 (CH). Molecular formula = C₆H₆.

1.3 Chemical Species
Chemical species are those species which take part in a chemical reaction e.g. atoms, molecules, ions, etc.
(i) Ion

An atom is a neutral particle as the number of electron and protons are equal in an atom. An atom can lose or gain electron and the balance between number of protons and electrons is disturbed. So there is net charge on the atom. The particle that carries an electrical charge, positive or negative due to the loss or gain of one or more electron is called an ion.
(i) Ion
There are two types of ions, a) Cation (Positive ions) and b) Anion (Negative ions).
a) Cation

The atom which loses electron(s) from its outer most shell, a net positive charge is appeared on that atom. This positively charged species is called cation. Positive ions always have less number of electrons than the number of proton. The following equations show the formation of cations from different atoms.
a) Cation
Atoms | | Cations; H | → | H⁺ + 1e⁻; Na | → | Na⁺ + 1e⁻; Mg | → | Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
b) Anion

The atom which gains electron(s), a net negative charge is appeared on the atom. This negatively charged species is called an anion. Negative ions always have more number of electrons than the number of protons. The following equations show the formation of anions from different atoms.
b) Anion
Atoms | | Anions; F + 1e⁻ | → | F⁻; Cl + 1e⁻ | → | Cl⁻; O + 2e⁻ | → | O²⁻

1.4.1 Avogadro's Number

A chemist deals with substances which are composed of large number of particles. It is not possible for the chemist to count these particles. The concept of Avogadro's number helped in the counting of these particles present in the given mass of a substance. Avogadro's number is collection of 6.023 × 10²³ particles.
1.4.1 Avogadro's Number
Avogadro's number is defined as the number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions) in one mole of any substance and is numerically equal to 6.023 × 10²³.
Scientific Information
The molecule made up of more than one atom are termed a: polyatomic molecules e.g.; diatomic = O₂; triatomic = CO₂; tetra atomic = NH₃; Penta atomic = CH₄
1.4.1 Avogadro's Number
This number was determined by an Italian scientist Amedo Avogadro and is called Avogadro's number represented by symbol “Nₐ”.
1.4.1 Avogadro's Number

Scientists are agreed that Avogadro's number of particles is present in one molar mass of a substance. In order to understand the relationship between the Avogadro's number and the mole of a substance, let's consider a few examples.
1.4.1 Avogadro's Number

i. 1.0 g of hydrogen = 1 mole = 6.023 × 10²³ atoms of hydrogen; ii. 12 g of carbon = 1 mole = 6.023 × 10²³ atoms of carbon; iii. 18 g of water = 1 mole = 6.023 × 10²³ molecules of water; iv. 58.5 g of NaCl = 1 mole = 6.023 × 10²³ formula unit of NaCl
Society, Technology and Science
In the mole concept, students often have trouble comprehending the huge size of Avogadro's number, 6.023 × 10²³. The following analogies may be helpful for better understanding of students.
Society, Technology and Science
If there were a mole of rice grains, all the land area in the whole world would be covered with rice to a depth of about 75 meters.
Society, Technology and Science
One mole of rice grains is more than all the grain that has been grown since the beginning of time.
Society, Technology and Science
A computer counting with a speed of 10 million atoms a second, would take two billion years to count one mole of atoms.
Society, Technology and Science
If one mole of marbles were spread over the surface of the Earth, our planet would be covered by a three miles thick layer of marbles.
1.4.2 Mole

We use different units in our daily life to represent different quantities of items so that we can count them easily. How do we count shoes? As shoes come in pairs, so we would most likely count them by pairs rather than individual shoes. Similarly eggs, banana etc are counted in dozens, but paper by reams. Thus, the counting unit depends on what we are counting.
1.4.2 Mole
Chemists also use a unit for counting atoms, molecules and ions. They use a counting unit called mole to measure the amount of a substance.
1.4.2 Mole

A mole is defined as the amount (mass) of a substance which contains Avogadro's number (6.023 × 10²³ particles). Mole is represented as ‘mol’. It forms a link between mass of substance and number of particles.

The mass of a substance is may be atomic mass, molecular mass or formula mass. These masses are expressed in atomic mass units (a.m.u.). But when these masses are expressed in grams they are called molar masses.

Society, Technology and Science

Over the course of human history, people have developed many interconnected and validated ideas about the physical, biological, psychological and social worlds. The means used to develop these ideas are particular ways of observing, thinking, experimenting and validating. These ways represent a fundamental aspect of the nature of science and reflect how science tends to differ from other modes of knowing.
Key Points

Chemistry is the branch of science, which deals with the composition, structure and properties of matter, the changes occurring in matter and the laws and principles under which these changes occur. • The main branches of chemistry are organic, inorganic, physical, analytical, industrial, nuclear, environmental and biochemistry. • Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass.
Key Points

• A piece of matter in pure form is called substance. • Matter can be classified as an element, a compound or a mixture. • An Element is a substance which cannot be split up into other simpler substances by any ordinary physical or chemical processes. • An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.
Key Points

• Compound is a pure substance made up of two or more elements chemically combined together in a fixed ratio by mass. • Mixtures can be classified as homogeneous or heterogeneous. • The atomic number (Z) of an element is the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom of that element. • The mass number (A) of an element is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom of that element.
Key Points
• Relative atomic mass of an element is the mass of an atom relative to mass of 1/12th of Carbon-12.
Key Points

An atomic mass unit is the mass of the 1/12 of the mass of any atom of Carbon-12. • Average atomic mass is the weighted average of the atomic masses of the naturally occurring isotopes of an element. • Chemical Formula is a shorthand method of representing a compound. Elemental symbols are used in writing a formula.
Key Points

• Empirical formula shows the smallest whole number ratio of the atoms/ions present, while molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms present in a molecule of the compound. • Molecular mass and formula mass of a compound is sum of the relative atomic masses of the elements (atoms) present in the compound. • Simple ions are atoms that have lost or gained electrons.
Key Points

• Molecules can also form ions called molecular ions. • Free radical is a specie, with an unpaired electron and is the result of homolytic fission of the bond. • A molecule is the smallest particle of a compound or element that can exist independently. It may be monoatomic or polyatomic. • Molecules made up of similar atoms are homoatomic and those composed of different atoms are hetero atomic.
Key Points

• A mole represents a definite quantity (mass) of an element or a compound. The gram atomic mass, gram formula mass or gram molecular mass of an element or compound is called a mole. • Avogadro's number is a constant value equal to 6.023 × 10²³ and this number of atoms or molecules is present in one mole of a substance.

He called them atoms. He presented his theory under the title 'A New System of Chemical Philosophy.'

2.1.1 Rutherford's Atomic Model
In 1911, Rutherford performed an experiment in order to know the arrangement of electrons and protons in an atom.
(i) Rutherford's Experiment/Discovery of Nucleus

Rutherford performed an experiment to determine the internal structure of the atom in 1911. For this purpose, he used a thin (0.00004cm) gold foil. The gold foil was surrounded by photographic plate or Zinc sulphide (ZnS) fluorescent screen to detect the particles emitting from the radiation.
(i) Rutherford's Experiment/Discovery of Nucleus

He bombarded the gold foil with approximately 20,000 α – particles from a radioactive source (polonium metal). He observed that about 19990 of the α – particles passed through the gold foil without any change in direction. It showed that most of the volume occupied by the atom is empty.
(i) Rutherford's Experiment/Discovery of Nucleus

Some α – particles (8) were deflected through smaller angle. Only few (2) were bounced back at their original way. Rutherford concluded that an atom contains a positive portion i.e. nucleus in the center of the atom. So, α – particles passing near this portion were repelled. Because, α – particles are also positively charged particles and similar charges repel each other.
(i) Rutherford's Experiment/Discovery of Nucleus
Fig: 2.3 Rutherford model of atom
(i) Rutherford's Experiment/Discovery of Nucleus

If α – particles pass very closely to nucleus, they deflected through large angles. Similarly, if they do not pass close to nucleus, they either get deflected through very small angles or do not get deflected at all.
(i) Rutherford's Experiment/Discovery of Nucleus

On the basis of his conclusion drawn from this experiment, he proposed a new model of atom called planetary model (similar to the solar system) which put all the protons in the nucleus and the electrons around the nucleus like planets around the sun.
(i) Rutherford's Experiment/Discovery of Nucleus
Fig: 2.4 Discovery of Nucleus
(ii) Main Points of Rutherford's Atomic Model
1. Atom consists of positively charged central portion called nucleus.
(ii) Main Points of Rutherford's Atomic Model
2. Electrons are revolving around the nucleus with very high speed just like the planets around the sun.
(ii) Main Points of Rutherford's Atomic Model
3. The size of the nucleus is very small as compared to the size of the atom and most of the volume occupied by the atom is empty.
(ii) Main Points of Rutherford's Atomic Model
4. Atom is neutral. As the number of electrons is numerically equal to that of protons.
(ii) Main Points of Rutherford's Atomic Model
5. Nucleus is responsible for mass and energy of the atom.

Rutherford in 1911, performed an experiment and proposed a model of an atom. These suggestions remained unchallenged for long time. But this model could not explain the stability of an atom and line spectrum for an atom. Bohr leaped over difficulty by using quantum theory of radiation that was proposed by Max Plank.

2.1.2 Neil Bohr's Atomic Theory

In 1913, Neil Bohr presented a new atomic theory to overcome the defects of Rutherford's atomic model. Bohr considered hydrogen atom as a model. This atomic model was based on the following assumptions.
2.1.2 Neil Bohr's Atomic Theory
1. Electrons are revolving around the nucleus in one of the fixed circular paths called shells or orbits. Each orbit has a fixed energy. These orbits are also called energy levels.
2.1.2 Neil Bohr's Atomic Theory
2. The energy of the electron in an orbit is proportional to its distance from the nucleus. The farther the electron from the nucleus, the higher will be the energy and vice versa.
2.1.2 Neil Bohr's Atomic Theory
3. As long as electrons are revolving around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits, they do not gain or lose energy .i.e. energy of an orbit is fixed.
2.1.2 Neil Bohr's Atomic Theory
4. When an electron jumps from a higher energy orbit to the lower energy orbit, it radiates energy and when it jumps from lower energy orbit to higher energy orbit, it absorbs energy.

5. Electron can reside in any one of the orbits and cannot stay in between them.

6. Angular momentum (mvr) of an electron is an integral multiple of h/(2π).

2.3 Isotopes

These are atoms of the same element which have same atomic number but different mass number. The difference in mass of an atom in an element is due to the difference in number of neutrons. In other words, we can say that these are the atoms of same element which have same number of protons and electrons but different number of Neutrons. Isotopes have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.
(i) Isotopes of Hydrogen

Hydrogen has three isotopes. These are Protium (H), Deuterium (D) and Tritium (T). Protium (H) is ordinary hydrogen. It is the most abundant isotope (99.985%) of hydrogen. Deuterium (D) is about 0.015 % and Tritium is rarely found in nature.
(i) Isotopes of Hydrogen

All the isotopes have one proton in their nuclei and one electron in their orbit, the difference lies in the number of neutrons. The number of neutrons in Protium (H) is zero, Deuterium (D) is one and Tritium (T) is two in its nucleus.
(i) Isotopes of Hydrogen
The chemical properties of the Isotopes are same due to the same number of valence electrons but there is difference in physical properties like density, melting point and boiling point etc.

Introduction

In previous grades, you have learnt about the elements and their classification on the basis of metals and non-metals. Using that knowledge, you will study the classification of all elements and will discuss their periodic properties.
Introduction

In the year 1800, only thirty four (34) elements were known. By the year 1870, this number increased to almost double and in the year 1974, the number of elements was 105. At present 118 elements are known. Out of 118 elements, 92 are found naturally on earth and the rest are artificially prepared.
Introduction

Initially the number of elements was limited so it was easy for chemists to study these elements individually. But as time passed, the number of elements increased, so it became difficult for the chemists to study each element individually. It was felt that the elements might be properly arranged so that they could be easily studied. By doing so, one could easily get more information with little effort.
Introduction

Many chemists, including Lavoisier (1787), Newlands (1864), and others attempted to classify the elements systematically. It was a Russian chemist Mendeleev (1869), who made the most successful classification based on the atomic masses of the elements.
Society, Technology and Science

The development of periodic table started in 1800. Many scientists in different ages attempted for classifying the elements in different ways. Initially elements were divided into metal and non-metals. In 1817, J. W. Dobereiner, a German chemist classified chemically similar elements in groups of three on the basis of their atomic masses. These groups are called triads.
Society, Technology and Science
In triads, the atomic weight of the middle element was the arithmetic mean of the atomic weights of the other two elements. For example, Li⁷, Na²³, K³⁹

atomic weight of Na = (7 + 39) / 2 = 23
Introduction

It failed to classify all the elements in this way. By 1864, more elements had been discovered. An English chemist J. Newland classified the elements in order of their increasing atomic masses. He classified the elements into groups of seven and found that every eighth element had the properties similar to the first one of the series. He called these groups octaves.
Introduction
Lithium (Li) resembles Sodium (Na) and fluorine (F) resembles chlorine (Cl), as shown below.
Introduction
He could not able to classify all the elements in the same manner, so the law of octaves failed to classify all the elements.
Introduction

In 1869, two chemists, Lothar Meyer in Germany and Dmitri Mendeleev in Russia, at about the same time independently developed very similar arrangements of the elements. They found that while arranging the elements in order of their increasing atomic mass, certain physical and chemical properties are repeated at regular intervals.
Introduction
Lothar Meyer plotted atomic volumes (densities) of the elements against their atomic masses and found that similar elements occupied similar positions in the graph.
Introduction

Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements in the form of table. He arranged 65 elements in periods and groups. In this table, he left vacant spaces for the elements which were not discovered at that time and to be placed in these vacant spaces. On the basis of this table, he predicted the properties of certain elements very accurately that were yet to be discovered.
Introduction

Mendeleev classification was based on atomic mass. However, with the discovery of atomic structure, it became clear that elements varied regularly with atomic number not with the atomic mass. It had also become known that the properties of the elements depended on the number and arrangement of electrons in each of its atom.
3.1 Modern Periodic Table

The modern periodic table was put forward by Henry Gwyn Jeffreys Moseley, an English physicist. This table is based on the atomic number. The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of the elements are the periodic function of their atomic number. Periodic table is formed on the basis of this law.
