3.4 LAWS OF LOGARITHM
There are four laws of logarithms. We shall prove them one by one as:
1. $\log_a mn = \log_a m + \log_a n$
Let $\log_a m = x \Rightarrow a^x = m\ \cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots(i)$ (By definition)
1. $\log_a mn = \log_a m + \log_a n$
and $\log_a n = y \Rightarrow a^y = n\ \cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots(ii)$ (By definition)
1. $\log_a mn = \log_a m + \log_a n$
Now, $mn = a^x \times a^y = a^{x+y}\ \Rightarrow\ a^{x+y} = mn\ \Rightarrow\ \log_a mn = x + y$
1. $\log_a mn = \log_a m + \log_a n$
Using (i) and (ii), we get $\log_a mn = \log_a m + \log_a n$
2. $\log_a \dfrac{m}{n} = \log_a m - \log_a n$
Here, $\dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{a^x}{a^y} = a^{x-y}\ \Rightarrow\ a^{x-y} = \dfrac{m}{n}\ \Rightarrow\ \log_a \dfrac{m}{n} = x - y$
2. $\log_a \dfrac{m}{n} = \log_a m - \log_a n$
Using (i) and (ii), we get $\log_a \dfrac{m}{n} = \log_a m - \log_a n$
3. $\log_a m^n = n\log_a m$
By (i), we have $a^x = m$
3. $\log_a m^n = n\log_a m$
Taking power $n$ both sides.
3. $\log_a m^n = n\log_a m$
$(a^x)^n = (m)^n\ \Rightarrow\ a^{xn} = m^n$
3. $\log_a m^n = n\log_a m$
$\Rightarrow\ \log_a m^n = nx$
3. $\log_a m^n = n\log_a m$
Using (i), we get $\log_a m^n = n\log_a m$
4. $\log_a m \log_m n = \log_a n$
Let $\log_a m = x \Rightarrow a^x = m\ \cdots\cdots\cdots(iii)$ (By definition)
4. $\log_a m \log_m n = \log_a n$
and $\log_m n = y \Rightarrow m^y = n\ \cdots\cdots\cdots(iv)$ (By definition)
4. $\log_a m \log_m n = \log_a n$
Now, $a^{xy} = (a^x)^y = m^y = n\ \Rightarrow\ a^{xy} = n\ \Rightarrow\ \log_a n = xy$
4. $\log_a m \log_m n = \log_a n$
using (i) and (ii), we get $\log_a m \log_m n = \log_a n$
Note
This law can also be written as: $\log_m n = \dfrac{\log_a n}{\log_a m}$
Note
This is called Change of Base Law.

SUMMARY

Introduction

In 820 AD., the Muslim mathematician, Al-Khwarizmi, wrote the algebraic text entitled Al-jabr Wa-Al Muqabala (the science of cancellation and reduction). A Latin translation of this text became known in Europe under the title Al-Jabr, became the word algebra. Al-Khwarizmi is known as the "Father of Algebra".
Introduction

Algebra uses special types of mathematical processes called algebraic operations. These operations include addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, extraction of roots and raising to integral or fractional powers.
4.1 ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS

When variables and constants are connected by the algebraic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, root extraction & rising integral or factional powers, the resulting expression so obtained is called an algebraic expression. For example
4.1 ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS

4.1 ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS

4.1 ALGEBRAIC EXPRESSIONS

Different parts of an algebraic expression which are combined together by the operations of addition and subtraction are called terms of the algebraic expression. For example in the algebraic expression $3x^2 + 5\sqrt{x} - 7$, the terms are $3x^2, 5\sqrt{x}, -7$.
4.1.1 Rational Expressions
An algebraic expression of the form $\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ where $p(x)$ & $q(x)$ are polynomials and $q(x) \neq 0$ is called a rational expression. For example;

4.1.1 Rational Expressions

Note

Every polynomial $p(x)$ can be regarded as a rational expression, since we can write $p(x)$ as $\dfrac{p(x)}{1}$. Thus every polynomial is a rational expression but every rational expression need not be a polynomial.
a) Polynomial or not

Every algebraic expression may not be a polynomial. For example $2x^2 + 7x + \dfrac{6}{x}$ with $x \neq 0$ is obviously an algebraic expression but it is not a polynomial. Similarly $\dfrac{1}{x + 3}$ with $x \neq -3$ is an algebraic expression but it is not a polynomial.
b) Rational expression or not

We know that a rational expression is always in the form $\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ where $p(x)$ & $q(x)$ are polynomials and $q(x) \neq 0$. Now $\sqrt{\dfrac{3x^2 - 5x - 2}{10 - x}}$ is an algebraic expression with $x \neq 10$. But it is not a rational expression because $\sqrt{\dfrac{3x^2 - 5x - 2}{10 - x}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3x^2 - 5x - 2}}{\sqrt{10 - x}}$.
b) Rational expression or not
Here $\sqrt{3x^2 - 5x - 2}$ and $\sqrt{10 - x}$ are not polynomials. Thus every algebraic expression is not a rational expression.

Let $a$ and $b$ be two integers, then $\dfrac{a}{b}$ may or may not be an integer (for example 2 and 5 are integers but $\dfrac{5}{2}$ is not an integer). Therefore, the set of integers is extended and $\dfrac{a}{b}$ where $b \neq 0$ and $a, b \in Z$ is defined as a rational number and thus we have a new set, the set of rational numbers.

4.3.1 Surds
A number of the form $\sqrt[n]{a}$, where $a$ is a positive rational number is called a surd.
4.3.1 Surds
A number, therefore, will be a surd if, and only if, (i) it is irrational and (ii) it is a root and (iii) a root of a rational number.
4.3.1 Surds

For example $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5 + \sqrt{3}}$ are both irrational numbers, but they are of different types. First number is a root of a rational number 3, whereas the second number is a root of an irrational number $5 + \sqrt{3}$. The number of the first type is a surd. The number $\sqrt[3]{8}$ is not a surd. It has a form of a surd number; but its value 2 is rational.
4.3.1 Surds
$\sqrt{-2}$, $\sqrt{-3}$ are not surds because $-2$ and $-3$ are negative.
4.3.2 Order of a Surd
In a surd $\sqrt[n]{a}$, $n$ is called the order of the surd or the surd index and $a$ is called the radicand.
4.3.2 Order of a Surd
Thus if n = 2 then it is called a surd of order 2 i.e. $\sqrt{a}$ is a surd of order 2.
4.3.2 Order of a Surd
If n = 3 then it is called surd of order 3 and if n = 4 then it is called surd of order 4 and so on.
4.3.2 Order of a Surd

Surds of second, third and fourth orders are called quadratic, cubic and biquadratic surds respectively. For example $\sqrt{5}, \sqrt[3]{7}, \sqrt[4]{3}$ are quadratic, cubic and biquadratic surds respectively.
4.3.2 Order of a Surd
Surds of the same order are called equiradical surds. For example $\sqrt[3]{5}, \sqrt[3]{2}$ are equiradical surds.
4.3.3 Types of a Surd
Surds are also named w.r.t to the number of terms. Surd expressions involving one, two, and three terms are called monomial, binomial and trinomial surds respectively.
4.3.3 Types of a Surd

For example $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{5} - 1$, $2 - \sqrt{7} + \sqrt{11}$ are monomial, binomial and trinomial surds respectively. In general expressions containing two or more surds are called compound [surds. Thus] $2 - \sqrt{7} + \sqrt{11}$ is a compound surd while $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{5} - 1$ are [not a com]pound surd.
4.3.3 Types of a Surd
If the coefficient of the surd is $\pm 1$, the surd is called an entire surd; otherwise it is known as a mixed surd.
4.3.3 Types of a Surd
For example $\sqrt{5}, \sqrt[3]{3}, \sqrt[4]{7}$ are entire surds and $-4\sqrt[3]{5}, \dfrac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{2}$ are mixed surds.
4.3.3 Types of a Surd

Surds which can be expressed as rational multiples of the same surd are called like or similar surds; and those which cannot be so expressed are called unlike or dissimilar. Thus $\sqrt{8}$, $\sqrt{18}$ are similar surds as they can be expressed as $\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$ and whereas $\sqrt{8}$, $\sqrt[3]{81}$, are unlike surds.
4.3.4 Conjugate Surds
Two binomial quadratic surds which differ only in the sign connecting their terms are called conjugate surds.
4.3.4 Conjugate Surds
Thus $a\sqrt{x} + b\sqrt{y}$ and $a\sqrt{x} - b\sqrt{y}$ are conjugate surds. These are always rationalizing factors of each other.
4.3.4 Conjugate Surds
i.e. $\left(a\sqrt{x} + b\sqrt{y}\right)\left(a\sqrt{x} - b\sqrt{y}\right) = a^2x - b^2y$
4.3.4 Conjugate Surds
Thus $5 + \sqrt{3}$ and $5 - \sqrt{3}$, $2 - \sqrt{5}$ and $2 + \sqrt{5}$ are called conjugate surds of each other.
4.4 RATIONALIZATION
The procedure of removing the surd quantity from the denominator of the surd fraction is very convenient and is known as the process of rationalizing the denominator or rationalization.
4.4 RATIONALIZATION
For purposes of calculating approximate values of surds, much tedious work can be saved by first rationalizing the surd expression.
4.4 RATIONALIZATION

For example, if it is required to find the numerical value of $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{3}}$ we have to find the value of $\sqrt{5}$ (i.e. 2.236), and the value of $\sqrt{3}$ (i.e. 1.732), and then obtain the quotient $\dfrac{2.236}{1.732}$, which is too tedious. Much of this labour can be saved by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{3}}$ by $\sqrt{3}$.

THEOREM 16.1
Parallelograms on the same base and lying between the same parallel lines (or of the same altitude) are equal in area.

Parallelograms ABCD and ABGH are equal in area.
Proof:

THEOREM 16.2
Parallelograms on equal bases and having the same altitude are equal in area.
Given:
ABCD and EFGH are two parallelograms having the same altitude (i.e. lying between the same parallel lines) and $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{EF}$.
To Prove:
The parallelograms are equal in area.

Statements | Reasons; $\overline{HG} \cong \overline{EF}$ | (Opposite sides of $\parallel^{gm}$); and $\overline{EF} \cong \overline{AB}$ | (Given); $\therefore \overline{AB} \cong \overline{HG}$ | (Transitive Property); But $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{HG}$ | (Lying on two parallel lines); $\therefore$ ABGH is a parallelogram | (Opposite sides parallel and congruent); Hence Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ ABCD $=$ Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ ABGH; Also Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ ABGH $=$ Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ EFGH; $\therefore$ Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ ABCD $=$ Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ EFGH | (Transitive Property)

Proof:

Proof:

| (Given); $\therefore$ Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ ABCD = Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ KLMN; But Area of $\triangle ABD = \dfrac{1}{2}$ Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ ABCD | (Diagonal bisects the $\parallel^{gm}$); and Area of $\triangle KLM = \dfrac{1}{2}$ Area of $\parallel^{gm}$ KLMN | (Diagonal bisects the $\parallel^{gm}$); Hence Area of $\triangle ABD$ = Area of $\triangle KLM$

A triangle has six elements, three sides and three angles. For example the elements of triangle the ABC are $AB$, $BC$, $AC$, $\angle ABC$ or $\angle B$, $\angle ACB$ or $\angle C$, $\angle BAC$ or $\angle A$.
The six elements of the triangle are:
1. Side AB. • 2. Side BC. • 3. Side AC. • 4. Angle ABC. • 5. Angle ACB. • 6. Angle BAC.
17.2 Construction of a Triangle in the following three cases
When two sides and the included angle are given. • When one side and two of the angles are given. • When two of its sides and the angle opposite to one of them are given.
To construct a triangle, when the lengths of two sides and measure of the included angle are given.
Steps of Construction:

1. Draw $\overline{PQ}$ of measure 4 cm. • 2. At P, construct an angle of $120^\circ$ with the help of a compass. • 3. With P as centre, draw an arc $\overline{PR}$ of radius 5 cm. i.e. $PR = 5$ cm. • 4. Join R to Q. PQR is the required triangle.
To construct a triangle when length of one side and measures of two of its angles are given.
Steps of Construction:
1. Draw $\overline{PQ}$ measuring 5.4cm. • 2. At P, draw an angle of $60^\circ$ and at Q, draw an angle of $45^\circ$. • 3. Let the two arms meet at R. • 4. PQR is the required triangle.
To construct a triangle when lengths of two of its sides and the measure of an angle opposite to one of these sides is given.
In this case, three possibilities can emerge.

a) When only one triangle can be constructed with the help of given data. • b) When two triangles can be constructed with the help of same data. • c) When construction of a triangle is not possible with the help of given data.
These possibilities are illustrated with the help of following example;
Steps of Construction:

1) Draw $\overline{AB}$ measuring 6cm. • 2) At A, construct $\angle BAD$ such that its measure is $30^\circ$. • 3) With B as center, draw an arc of radius 3cm. • 4) The arc intersects $\overrightarrow{AD}$ at only one-point C. • 5) Join C to B. • 6) ABC is the required triangle.
Steps of Construction:

1) Draw $\overline{KL}$ such that $m\overline{KL} = 6.5$ cm. • 2) At L construct an $\angle KLX = 45^\circ$. • 3) With K as centre, draw an arc of radius 5.5cm to intersect $\overrightarrow{LX}$ at M and M'. • 4) Join K to M and M'. • 5) KLM and KLM' are the required triangles.
Steps of Construction:

1) Draw $\overline{YZ}$ measuring 6.5cm. • 2) At Y, construct $\angle ZYA$ such that $m\angle ZYA = 60^\circ$. • 3) With Z as center, draw an arc of radius 4cm ($= m\overline{ZX}$). • 4) The arc does not intersect the arm $\overrightarrow{YA}$ of $\angle Y$.
Steps of Construction:
In this case, no triangle can be constructed to satisfy the given data.
From these examples it can be concluded that if lengths of two sides and an angle (which is not included angle) are given, then there can be:
i) One triangle, or • ii) Two triangles, or • iii) no triangle at all.
17.2.4 Concurrent lines and point of Concurrency
i) Two coplanar lines are either parallel or intersecting. • ii) Two lines intersect each other at one and only one point, which is called their point of intersection.
Tidbit
Three or more lines are said to be concurrent, if they pass through the same point.
17.2.4 Concurrent lines and point of Concurrency
Now, if a third line also passes through the same point of intersection, then the three lines are said to be concurrent. Point through which these three lines pass is called the point of concurrency.
Remember
A line, which divides a given angle into two angles of equal measure, is called 'angle bisector'.
Steps of Construction:

1. Draw $\overline{BC}$ measuring 5cm. • 2. With B and C as centers and radii respectively equal to 4.6 and 5.1, draw arcs intersecting at A. • 3. Draw $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$. • 4. Draw bisector of angles A, B and C. These bisectors pass through the same point I. Thus, angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent.
Remember
A perpendicular drawn from a vertex of a triangle to its opposite side is called 'altitude' of the triangle.
Steps of Construction:

1. Construct $\triangle ABC$ with the help of given data. • 2. Draw perpendiculars from A to $\overline{BC}$, B to $\overline{CA}$ and C to $\overline{AB}$. • 3. $\overline{AD}$, $\overline{BE}$ and $\overline{CF}$ are the required altitudes.
Steps of Construction:
We see that the three altitudes pass through the same point O. i.e. altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.

Steps of Construction:
All the three perpendicular bisectors pass through C. i.e. they are concurrent.

Practical geometry is the relationship between theory and practice. • Engineers, architects and builders make use of practical geometry before they build buildings, bridges and other structures. • In practical geometry, a construction is a drawing made with the straight edge and compass. Parallelograms on the same base and lying between the same parallel lines (or of the same altitude) are equal in area.
SUMMARY

• A triangle has six elements, three sides and three angles. • Two coplanar lines are either parallel or intersecting. • Two lines intersect each other at one and only one point, which is called their point of intersection. • Angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent. • Altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.
SUMMARY

By tolerance we mean a fair and objective attitude towards those whose lifestyle differs from ours. Tolerance is the virtue which enables a person to forebear the attitude, negative remarks and action with patience and calmness. The life of Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) is a superb example of tolerance. It is his tolerance that let him forgive his worst enemies.
Reading
Truly, he is an epitome of tolerance, forgiveness, patience and compassion. The Holy Quran describes him as Rahmatul-lil-Alameen, (a mercy unto the whole mankind and universe.)
2. Boycott at Shab-Abi-Talib & Peaceful Entry into Makkah

While preaching Islam in Makkah, the Quraish ostracised him and his family Banu-Hashim. They lived in a valley called Shab-Abi-Talib. There was scarcity of food and water. The believers had no means of income and they were leading a very tough life for a period of three years.
2. Boycott at Shab-Abi-Talib & Peaceful Entry into Makkah
During this situation Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) remained calm and tolerant and never thought about taking any sort of revenge.
2. Boycott at Shab-Abi-Talib & Peaceful Entry into Makkah

Even after he had conquered Makkah, Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) taught his followers to remain tolerant. After the conquest of Makkah, the Muslim army entered Makkah humbly and peacefully. No house was robbed; no man or woman was insulted. Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) granted a general amnesty to the entire population of Makkah.
3. Assembly at Khana-e-Kaaba & Words of Hazrat Yousuf (AS)
After conquest of Makkah, when everybody gathered in Khana-e-Kaaba, Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) asked the people of Quraish, "What do you expect at my hands?"
3. Assembly at Khana-e-Kaaba & Words of Hazrat Yousuf (AS)
They all shouted in one voice, "Kindness and pity, gracious brother, gracious nephew". They were not disappointed.
3. Assembly at Khana-e-Kaaba & Words of Hazrat Yousuf (AS)

Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) said the same forgiving words as Hazrat Yousuf (علیہ السلام) had said to his brothers, "Have no fear this day, May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy".
3. Assembly at Khana-e-Kaaba & Words of Hazrat Yousuf (AS)

He even forgave Abu Sufyan and his wife who were the worst enemies of Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) and Islam. He plotted many times against the Rasool (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) but Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) never did so.
4. The Incident of Rabbi Zaid ibn Sanah

Similarly, the story of the Rabbi Zaid is one such epitome of learning from Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) practices, which reflects tolerance towards others. Once Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) was attending funeral of a man from the Ansar. Hazrat Abu Bakr, Hazrat Umar, Hazrat Usman and some other companions were with him.
4. The Incident of Rabbi Zaid ibn Sanah

After the funeral prayer the Rasool (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) sat down close to a wall, and a Jewish Rabbi, Zaid ibn Sanah came towards him, he grabbed the Rasool (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) by the edges of his cloak, looked at him in a harsh way, and said, "O Muhammad! Will you not pay me back my loan? I have not known the family of Abdul-Mutalib to delay in repaying debts."
4. The Incident of Rabbi Zaid ibn Sanah

After seeing what the Rabbi did to Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ), Hazrat Umar's eyes swelled with anger, he looked at the Rabbi and said: "O enemy of Allah, do you talk to the Messenger of Allah and behave towards him in this manner?"
4. The Incident of Rabbi Zaid ibn Sanah

The Rabbi turned away and Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) said to Hazrat Umar, "You should have given us sincere counselling, rather than act as you did! Go and repay him his loan, and give him twenty Sa'a (a measurement of weight) extra because you scared him."
5. Testing the Prophet's Tolerance & Acceptance of Islam

Hazrat Umar went to the Rabbi, repaid him the debt, and gave him an extra twenty Sa'a of dates. The Rabbi asked Hazrat Umar why and he replied, "The messenger of Allah ordered me to give it to you because I frightened you."
5. Testing the Prophet's Tolerance & Acceptance of Islam

The fact was that Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) was not late in repaying the debt, the Rabbi was asking for the repayment days before the loan was due because he wanted to test Hazrat Muhammad's tolerance. The Rabbi Zaid found that tolerance and perseverance took precedence over anger and that harsh treatment was repaid with kindness.
5. Testing the Prophet's Tolerance & Acceptance of Islam
The Rabbi Zaid immediately renounced his religion and testified before Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ):
5. Testing the Prophet's Tolerance & Acceptance of Islam
'There is none worthy of worship but Allah alone and that Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) is His Rasool.'
6. Boundless Character: Mercy, Kindness and Compassion

The tolerance of Hazrat Muhammad (رسول اللہ خاتم النبیین ﷺ) knew no bounds. He always treated people with kindness and compassion. Violence, anger and rudeness were never part of his method nor were they part of his character. He showed tolerance in the face of adversity and kindness in the face of harsh treatment.

Present Perfect Continuous Tense

This tense expresses an action that started in past and still continues in present. It is used to state an ongoing action that has started at a point in the past. A time-reference is also used in the sentence to show that when the action started in past or for how long the action continued.
Present Perfect Continuous Tense

The specific words 'since' and 'for' are used in sentence to show the time of action. The word 'since' is used if the exact starting time of action is known or intended to be reflected in the sentence (e.g. since Monday, since 3 P.M). The word 'for' is used to express the duration of time for which the action was continued (e.g. for three hours, for six months).
Present Perfect Continuous Tense
Structure of Sentence: Has/have + been + present participle
Past Perfect Continuous Tense

Past Perfect Progressive tense is used to describe an ongoing action that started in past and continued for some time in past. It expresses continued nature of an action that started and stopped at some point in the past. The sentence includes a 'time-reference' to show that when the action started in past or for how long the action was continued in past.

The world of living things can be grouped according to similarities and differences. Animal scientists do this by studying how members of the animal kingdom are alike. This is not always an easy task. Even within the same group of animals there may be surprising differences. For example, while most mammals are land-living animals, some like the bat are flying creatures.
The World of Living Things

The aquatic mammals, such as the whale and the dolphin, move from place to place by swimming. Others, like the mole, are digging animals that use their burrows for escaping from predators. Therefore the animals’ “moving in different ways” is not a very useful method of classifying them.
The World of Living Things
Instead, scientists rely on the classifying of a wider group of features, such as whether the animal has a backbone (vertebrates) or not (invertebrates).

Adverbial phrases. An adverbial phrase is a group of words that act together as an adverb, giving more information about a verb, adjective, or other adverb in a sentence. The adverbial phrase answers the same questions as a regular adverb: how/how much, when, or where.
Writing

Adverbial clauses in sentences. An adverb clause, like all clauses, has a verb and usually a subject. It is connected to the rest of the sentence with a subordinating conjunction, such as because, when, if, or although. Because it contains a subordinating conjunction, the adverb phrase is a dependent clause: it cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. It functions much as a single word adverb does:
Writing
modifying a verb, adjective, or another adverb. However, an adverb clause may also modify an entire clause or phrase. It describes where, when, why, how, or how much something is happening.
Writing

Story Review: The Conflict between Quality Craftsmanship and Commercial Advertising in 'The Fantastic Shoemake

John Galsworthy's narrative, adapted as 'The Fantastic Shoemaker', presents a haunting critique of modern industrial capitalism. Zarin Gul represents the pre-industrial artisan whose identity is inseparable from his art. For him, a pair of boots is not a disposable commodity but a masterpiece of integrity. However, modern advertising prioritizes superficial appearance and rapid turnover over durable quality.
Story Review: The Conflict between Quality Craftsmanship and Commercial Advertising in 'The Fantastic Shoemake

Galsworthy illustrates how unregulated market forces ruthlessly crush small, honest artisans in favor of profit-driven corporations. Zarin Gul's death is not merely personal tragedy; it symbolizes the death of human artistry in an era of mechanical mass consumption.

Summary of the Poem 'The Old Woman'
Poem Summary

Content: In 'The Old Woman', Joseph Campbell pays a tender, lyrical tribute to the beauty, dignity, and serenity of old age. The poet asserts that true beauty does not vanish with youth; rather, it transforms into a higher spiritual grace. In the first stanza, Campbell compares an elderly woman's wrinkled face to a pure white candle glowing in a holy shrine, symbolizing purity, sanctity, and reverence.
Poem Summary

In the second stanza, her state is likened to the spent radiance of the winter sun. Having completed her life's grueling toil ('travail done') and raised her family, her presence radiates soothing, mild warmth. In the final stanza, her children have grown up and departed ('her brood gone from her').
Poem Summary

Free from domestic turmoil, her mind rests in deep contemplation, as serene and unruffled as the still pool of water beneath a ruined watermill. The poem beautifully captures the peace, fulfillment, and divine tranquility that crown a life of selfless devotion.

Content: Nestled beneath the towering, snow-capped pinnacle of Tirich Mir (7,708 m) in the mighty Hindu Kush range, Chitral Valley is one of Pakistan's most enchanting alpine paradises. The valley is renowned worldwide for its pristine turquoise rivers, lush fruit orchards of walnuts, apples, and apricots, and the unique, ancient culture of the Kalash people living in Bumburet, Rumbur, and Birir.
Chitral Valley Description

The Kalash maintain vibrant polytheistic traditions, wearing intricately embroidered black dresses and celebrating seasonal festivals like Chilimjusht with rhythmic folk dances. Chitral's rugged mountain trails are home to the majestic Markhor and elusive snow leopards.

Persuasive Essay Nature
Part C: Persuasive Essay — The Imperative Need for the Preservation of Nature
Persuasive Essay Nature

Content: Nature is not a commodity that belongs to humanity; humanity belongs to nature. The intricate web of biodiversity—forests, wetlands, alpine ranges, and wildlife—provides the foundational ecosystem services essential for human survival: clean air, potable water, fertile soil, and climate stability.
Persuasive Essay Nature

Yet, through unchecked industrial pollution and deforestation, modern civilization is dismantling the very life-support systems of our planet. Firstly, biodiversity loss threatens global food security and public health. Forests purify air by sequestering millions of tons of carbon dioxide, while mangrove wetlands shield coastal communities from catastrophic cyclones.
Persuasive Essay Nature

When ecosystems collapse, zoonotic diseases spread rapidly and agricultural soils degrade into barren wastelands. Secondly, deforestation and fossil-fuel consumption have accelerated global warming, causing disastrous floods and heatwaves. In Pakistan, melting glaciers and erratic monsoons have displaced millions. Saving nature is therefore a matter of national survival.
Persuasive Essay Nature

We must urgently enforce strict anti-poaching laws, transition to renewable green energy, eliminate single-use plastics, and implement nationwide reforestation drives. Let us act decisively today, so that our children inherit a living, blooming Earth rather than a desolate wasteland.

Parentheses

Parentheses add emphasis to the words contained in the parentheses. One way parentheses are used in writing is to give information that might interrupt the normal flow of the sentence. Sometimes this information adds to reader’s understanding of the rest of the sentence. Parenthesis (round brackets) is used to:
Parentheses
enclose numbers or letters in enumerations in the text • express an amount in numbers previously expressed in words • mark off explanatory or supplementary material

Example: Hameed Ullah Khan (the architect) built castles and bridges. The information in the parentheses, called a parenthetical element, may also be information that is unrelated to the sentence or unnecessary.
Ellipsis

An ellipsis is a series of three dots (...) which shows that some text has been left out. The ellipsis is used to shorten a passage. The omitted text does not change the meaning of the original text and is unnecessary to its meaning. It may also be used to show a pause, a hesitation, or an incomplete thought, especially in quotations. Note there is a space before and after the ellipsis.
Ellipsis
If the ellipsis is at the end of a quotation followed by a speaker reference, there is no comma.

Poem Summary
Summary of 'Abou Ben Adhem'
Poem Summary

Content: In this inspiring narrative poem, Leigh Hunt illustrates the sublime spiritual truth that loving humanity is the most direct pathway to earning God's love. One night, Abou Ben Adhem, a pious and peaceful man, awakens to see an angel bathed in silvery moonlight, writing in a golden book. Abou respectfully asks what the angel is writing.
Poem Summary

The angel gently replies that it is listing the names of those who love God. Upon learning that his own name is not included, Abou remains undismayed and humbly requests to be recorded as one who loves his fellow human beings. The next night, the angel returns surrounded by a glorious, awakening light and shows the names of those blessed by God's divine love—and Abou Ben Adhem's name leads all the rest.
Poem Summary
The poem beautifully concludes that selfless service to humanity is the supreme act of worship.
Essay Haqooq Ul Ebad
Essay: Haqooq-ul-Ebad — Rights of Fellow Human Beings (100–150 Words)
Essay Haqooq Ul Ebad

Content: In Islamic jurisprudence and universal ethics, human duties are broadly categorized into two spheres: 'Haqooq-Allah' (the Rights of Allah, such as prayer and fasting) and 'Haqooq-ul-Ebad' (the Rights of Fellow Human Beings).
Essay Haqooq Ul Ebad

While Almighty Allah may forgive shortcomings in His personal worship out of His infinite mercy, He has ordained that violations against fellow human beings will not be forgiven until the wronged individual pardons them.
Essay Haqooq Ul Ebad

Haqooq-ul-Ebad encompasses treating parents with utmost kindness, supporting orphans, aiding neighbors regardless of faith, providing charity to the poor, maintaining honesty in business, and safeguarding others from harm. Serving suffering humanity is the greatest manifestation of faith. A society grounded in Haqooq-ul-Ebad fosters universal brotherhood, social justice, and lasting peace.

Moral Essay: Service to Humanity as the Highest Manifestation of True Worship

Leigh Hunt's immortal poem 'Abou Ben Adhem' provides a profound ethical philosophy: that love for the Creator is inseparable from love for His creation. In religious practices across world faiths, individuals often focus solely on ritualistic devotion while remaining indifferent to the poverty, illness, and suffering around them.

However, authentic faith requires transforming spiritual devotion into practical humanitarian action. Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) taught: 'The best of people are those who are most beneficial to people.'
